paper_title: Reading, Writing, Sharing, and Interacting with the World through Video

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Video foundation models have advanced rapidly in understanding and generating visual sequences, while video world models seek to capture the underlying dynamics of the world they depict. Despite their different objectives, both concern the relationship between video observations and an evolving world. This survey adopts world modeling as a unifying lens for examining these developments. Viewing an observed video as a partial, lossy, and temporally ordered projection of a latent temporal world, we organize the literature around four complementary operations: reading infers world properties from observed video; writing synthesizes video from specified or learned world conditions; sharing integrates understanding and generation through common modeling mechanisms; and interacting predicts and updates world states under actions and evolving observations. This perspective distinguishes temporal coherence in observed or generated sequences from consistency in the underlying world state. Across tasks, representations, models, datasets, and benchmarks, we trace a shift in emphasis from clip-level recognition and perceptual fidelity toward persistent state, controllable evolution, physical and causal validity, and evaluation grounded in interaction and downstream decisions, and we distill the open challenges that follow.

sections.title: 1 Introduction
sections.content: Vision is the process of discovering from images what is present in the world, and where it is. David Marr, Vision, 1982 [338] Video occupies distinctive position among the modalities available to machine intelligence. Unlike static images that capture individual moments, text that conveys selectively described information, or audio that primarily records acoustic dynamics, video directly captures how visible entities, their relations, and actions evolve across space and time, often together with synchronized audio, speech, and text. This rich spatiotemporal information makes video essential to wide range of applications, including communication, entertainment, autonomous driving, robotics, healthcare, and education. Consequently, video has long been central subject of computer vision and multimedia research, progressing from spatiotemporal architectures for action recognition [39, 102, 208] to self-supervised pretraining for transferable video representations [453, 482]. More recently, advances in large language models (LLMs) and large-scale generative modeling have driven shift from task-specific video models toward general-purpose video foundation models, expanding their capabilities along three complementary directions. For video understanding, Video-LLMs such as Video-LLaVA [271] enable language-based interaction with visual sequences, while Qwen3-VL [12] extends multimodal context to 256K tokens to accommodate longer video inputs. For video generation, models such as Sora [31], Wan [462], HunyuanVideo [219], Movie Gen [372], and Seedance 2.0 [442] demonstrate increasingly capable synthesis under diverse conditions, with Sora and Loong [487] further exploring minutescale generation. Toward the unification of understanding and generation, emerging models [479, 498, 531] seek to integrate these capabilities through shared token representations, latent spaces, or modeling interfaces, bringing video perception and synthesis into common foundation-model framework. Beyond video understanding and generation, broader research direction is emerging around modeling how the physical world evolves, rather than merely interpreting or synthesizing its visual observations. Although language models acquire extensive knowledge through text, their representations are only indirectly grounded in physical experience, motivating the pursuit of world models that can predict how an environment changes over time and support reasoning and planning [59, 229]. This idea has roots in model-based reinforcement learning, where agents learn predictive dynamics to simulate possible futures and evaluate candidate actions before acting [143, 146]. Video provides natural and scalable foundation for extending this paradigm beyond task-specific environments: by capturing continuous changes in objects, relations, and actions, large-scale video data offers rich supervision for learning world dynamics without requiring manually annotated labels, although actions and underlying physical states often remain unobserved. Building on this opportunity, recent research has explored several complementary approaches to video-based world modeling. Generative models such as Sora [31] have motivated the prospect of learning world dynamics through video synthesis, while Genie [32] demonstrates how interactive environments can be learned from unlabeled videos. Actionand condition-aware models such as GAIA-1 [172] and Cosmos [355] extend predictive generation toward driving and physical AI, whereas V-JEPA 2 [9] and Dreamer 4 [147] explore predictive representations and imagined trajectories for planning and control. Together with progress in interactive simulation [561], egocentric and robotic learning [133, 511], and long-horizon prediction [528], these developments are expanding the role of video from medium for perception and generation toward foundation for predicting and interacting with dynamic environments. Figure 1 traces milestones of these lines of work. These two lines of progress are increasingly converging around common challenge: connecting video observations with the dynamics of the world they depict. Video world models must infer underlying states from observed sequences before predicting how those states evolve, and often translate predicted states back into visual observations for simulation, evaluation, or planning. Conversely, video generators are increasingly incorporating actionand state-dependent controls, while unified video models explicitly couple visual understanding with synthesis. Despite their different objectives, these approaches therefore share fundamental question: what relationship does model learn between an observed video and the evolving world that gives rise to it? To examine this question systematically, we adopt world modeling as unifying perspective on video foundation models. Specifically, we view an observed video as partial, lossy, and temporally ordered observation 6 Video Foundation Models World-Modeling Lens of an underlying latent temporal world . This distinction provides common basis for organizing four complementary research paradigms: reading, which infers world properties from observed video; (cid:210) writing, which synthesizes video observations from specified or learned world conditions; sharing, which integrates both directions within unified modeling framework; and (cid:132) interacting, which updates or predicts world states in response to actions and evolving observations. These paradigms characterize different ways in which models connect video observations to the underlying world, rather than merely categorizing models by their input and output modalities. This perspective enables systematic comparison of their objectives, capabilities, and evaluation criteria while preserving the distinctions between visual plausibility, temporal coherence, and consistency of the modeled world. Section 2 formalizes this framework and clarifies how these properties differ across the four paradigms. Existing relevant surveys have examined related developments from different perspectives, including general world models organized around predictive state representations across modalities [84], interactive video world models centered on online prediction and control [286, 320], 3D and 4D world modeling grounded in explicit geometric representations [218], multimodal language models emphasizing the integration of visual encoders and language reasoning [581], long-form video generation focusing on temporal extension and consistency [240], and audio-visual foundation models spanning complementary modalities [384]. While these surveys provide valuable insights into individual research directions, they do not collectively establish unified account of how video models connect observations to evolving world states across understanding, generation, unification, and interaction. Our survey addresses this gap by taking the relation between video observations and the underlying dynamic world as its central organizing principle, not any single architecture, task, or modality. Under this perspective, we systematically examine the four paradigms of reading, writing, sharing, and interacting through common analytical framework. For each paradigm, we review the tasks, datasets, and evaluation protocols that define its objectives; the representations and model architectures that support its capabilities; the reasoning and control mechanisms that extend its functionality; and the applications that demonstrate its practical utility. Beyond reviewing individual paradigms, we identify several cross-cutting questions: how models represent and preserve world states beyond immediate observations, how actions and external conditions influence state evolution, and how predictive capabilities translate into effective reasoning and decision-making. These questions also motivate closer examination of evaluation practices, particularly the distinction between conventional metrics of recognition accuracy or perceptual fidelity and emerging criteria concerning state persistence, controllability, physical and causal consistency, and downstream utility. Within the interacting paradigm, we further distinguish video world models along two complementary dimensions: prediction space, ranging from observation-space to latent-state prediction, and transition interface, ranging from passive prediction to action-conditioned rollout and closed-loop interaction. This taxonomy separates what model predicts from how its predictions are conditioned, updated, and used. Our review covers publicly available research that contributes relevant architectural, methodological, or evaluation evidence. We retain foundational studies where necessary to establish conceptual and technical developments, while interpreting recent advances in the context of their specific tasks, training data, and evaluation protocols. Throughout the survey, we distinguish between the capabilities supported by models design, the supervision provided by its training data, and the empirical evidence demonstrated by its evaluation, avoiding assumptions that strong performance on individual video tasks necessarily implies consistent or generalizable world modeling. Specifically, this survey makes three main contributions: world-modeling lens. The four-operation framework of reading, writing, sharing, and interacting relates video understanding, video generation, unified video models, and video world models in one account, plus two-axis classification of world models by prediction space and transition interface. comprehensive scope with insights. Across tasks, representations, models, systems, datasets, and benchmarks, we compare how the four operations represent state, learn from video, accept control, preserve memory, and are evaluated. The synthesis distills recurring design patterns and failure modes into explicit insights, and identifies open directions, including long-horizon consistency, physical and causal grounding, measurable synergy between understanding and generation, and standardized evaluation of world properties. sections.title: 2 The World-Modeling Lens
sections.content: This section defines the world and its video (Section 2.1), two forms of consistency used later for evaluation (Section 2.2), and the four operations that organize Sections 47 (Section 2.3). Table 1 lists the notation. 9 Video Foundation Models World-Modeling Lens

sections.title: 2.1 World, Video, and Represented State
sections.content: We distinguish three objects: the evolving world, the video through which it is observed, and the representations that model constructs from available information. The following definitions provide conceptual abstraction: Definition 2.1 (Latent temporal world) The latent temporal world is stochastic process = (wt)t1 over state space W. Each state wt encompasses entities, their attributes and relations, and relevant physical and dynamic variables. Assuming that wt contains sufficient information for predicting subsequent evolution, its dynamics can be expressed as where at denotes an optional intervention or control input, with uncontrolled evolution recovered when no such input is supplied. wt+1 ( wt, at), Definition 2.2 (Observed video) An observed video = (x1, . . . , xT ) is temporally ordered sequence of visual observations generated by sensing process, xt O( wt, πt), where πt is the camera configuration. We refer to an observed or generated video as trace. This trace is partial : xt depends only on the part of wt visible under πt, which changes with camera motion, shot changes, or multiple cameras; lossy: sensing, resolution, compression, and editing remove information, so distinct world states may produce indistinguishable observations; and temporally ordered : frame order and duration carry evidence about motion and state transition, and thus about . Definition 2.3 (Represented state) model with parameters θ may construct an internal representation st qθ( xt, a<t), inferred from the observations and actions available up to time t; deterministic encoder st = fθ(xt, a<t) is the special case of point mass, and transition model may instead sample st+1 from its own predictions (Definition 2.6). In general, st = wt, and its information about the underlying world may be incomplete or inaccurate. Remark. Definitions 2.12.3 describe partially observable dynamical system, closely related to the environment model underlying partially observable Markov decision process. Such formulations are widely used in model-based reinforcement learning [143, 146], where agents infer predictive states from observations and simulate possible futures under candidate actions. For general video foundation models, however, the represented state may be implicit or constructed from an entire sequence rather than updated online.

sections.title: 2.2 Two Forms of Consistency
sections.content: Because video observes the world only partially (Definition 2.2), trace can be consistent at two levels. Definition 2.4 (Temporal coherence and world consistency) Let ˆV = (ˆx1, . . . , ˆxT ) be trace that model generates or predicts. ˆV is temporally coherent if neighboring frames agree locally, d(ˆxt, ˆxt+1) δ for all t, where penalizes implausible local motion, appearance change, or flicker. ˆV is world-consistent relative to specified dynamics and constraints, if its observations are compatible with at least one admissible world trajectory: w1:T C, π1:T s.t. ˆxt supp O( wt, πt), t, where contains the trajectories that satisfy the assumed dynamics, identity persistence, spatial relations, and relevant physical and causal constraints under the specified interventions. When the camera path is specified as condition, π1:T is fixed to it instead of quantified. 10 Video Foundation Models World-Modeling Lens Observation 2.5 (Coherence-consistency) Neither property implies the other. An object that changes identity after leaving the frame, room that alters its layout between visits, or an action whose effect later disappears can yield locally smooth frames that no trajectory in explains; conversely, hard cut violates local smoothness while remaining world-consistent. Temporal coherence is property of the trace; world consistency is property of the world the trace implies. recorded video is world-consistent by construction, because real trajectory produced it, so the distinction matters for traces that model writes or predicts. World-modeling evidence must therefore test world consistency, not only temporal coherence. As and are unobserved, Definition 2.4 is an evaluation target, not metric; benchmarks in Sections 5.1.2 and 7.4 probe it via revisits, occlusion, and interventions.

sections.title: 2.3 The Four Operations
sections.content: Definition 2.6 (Four operations) Reading (video comprehension). Reading infers selected properties of the world from observed video, ˆϕt rθ( st), an estimate of ϕ(wt), where st is constructed from the available observations and ϕ ranges over semantic, spatial, temporal, physical, and causal properties. It is evaluated by accuracy against ϕ(wt) and by calibrated uncertainty for occluded or off-screen content. (cid:210) Writing (video generation). Writing samples trace from condition, ˆx1:T pθ(x1:T c), where (text, an image or video prefix, audio, camera motion, trajectories, or layouts) specifies the world only in part and the generator resolves the rest. It is evaluated by perceptual quality, adherence to c, and world consistency of ˆV (Definition 2.4). Sharing (unified comprehension and generation). Sharing couples reading map with parameters θR and writing map with parameters θW through at least one shared component: parameters (θR θW = ), tokens or representations, an interface, or training objective. It is evaluated at three levels: capability coverage, architectural sharing, and functional synergy, that is, measurable improvement of reading, writing, or both under matched resources. (cid:132) Interacting (video world modeling). Interacting rolls out transition model, st+1 pθ(st+1 st, at, ct), with ˆxt+1 = gθ(st+1) when visible output is needed. The state st may be frames, video tokens, or latent features, and the actions at and conditions ct are fixed before an open-loop rollout or supplied online. It is evaluated by whether predicted changes follow these inputs and stay world-consistent (Definition 2.4), beyond the quality of rendered frames. The arrows here are conceptual shorthand: writing reaches only through c, and reading and writing are not exact inverses. Stronger claims about the represented state need stronger evidence; Table 2 gives four levels for each operation, from plausible output to decision utility. One system can perform several operations: unified editor reads source clip before writing its revision, and an interactive world model reads its history, writes each next frame, and updates its state in one backbone. Figure 1 places milestones of the four lines of work on one timeline, from video encoders [8, 102] and generators [162, 169] to unified models [479, 531] and action-conditioned simulators [32, 172].

sections.title: 3 Preliminaries
sections.content: This section covers the background shared by the four operations: video scenarios (Section 3.1), video large language models (Section 3.2), generative modeling (Section 3.3), and the scope and taxonomy of video world models (Section 3.4).

sections.title: 3.1 Video Scenarios
sections.content: Video modeling spans diverse scenarios that differ in temporal extent, observation perspective, modality composition, information availability, interaction, and domain-specific constraints. Rather than forming mutually exclusive categories, these characteristics impose complementary demands on what model must 11 Video Foundation Models World-Modeling Lens Table 2 Evidence ladder for claims about the world. Table 3 lists the evidence, modeling demands, and representative resources of each scenario. Three labels describe the recorded content: its default form, its modalities, and its viewpoint. Regular short video, the standard setting for representation learning and clip-level understanding, consists of passive thirdperson clips of seconds to minutes, whose audio is usually ignored. Its datasets annotate action classes [208], actions defined by temporal change [132], or captions [541], but do not test memory, online response, or control. Sounding video treats synchronized audio as evidence, with tasks that range from audio-event recognition and source localization to generating events whose sound and appearance must agree [50, 124, 449]. Its benchmarks must rule out visual or language shortcuts. Egocentric video is recorded from wearers or agents viewpoint, so hands, manipulated objects, gaze, and body-coupled camera motion enter the stream [78, 133, 134, 336]. The task shifts from recognizing actions to tracking object state and intent across long activities with frequent occlusion. Three further labels describe how the model accesses observations and whether it can change them. In streaming and online video, frames arrive incrementally, so model must update its state and respond within bounded latency, without access to future frames. Typical tasks are online question answering and streaming captioning, which may require timestamped or proactive responses [352, 569]. The same recording can be processed offline in full or presented as stream. Long-form video spans minutes to hours: the full recording is usually available, but not every frame can be processed at full resolution, and the evidence for query is sparse and spread across distant segments [109, 472, 509, 654]. model must therefore decide which evidence to keep and link events that lie far apart in time. Interactive video lets human, policy, or agent supply actions that change what is observed next [7, 406, 575]. Unlike in passive stream, the future then depends on the interaction history; interactive world models (Section 3.4) target this setting. Domain-specific video cuts across all of these labels: driving [33, 416], surgery [456], sports [127], and instructional video [343, 437] impose their own event structure, terminology, and costs of error. These domains test whether general video representations transfer to rare events and specialized outputs.

sections.title: 3.2 Video Large Language Models
sections.content: Connecting video to an LLM. Video-LLM feeds video into pretrained large language model (LLM), usually an autoregressive Transformer [454, 460] trained by next-token prediction (Equation (2)). Because the context window is fixed and also holds the instructions, earlier dialogue, and the output, long-video models must split the remaining budget between temporal coverage and visual detail.

sections.title: 3.4 Taxonomy of Video World Models
sections.content: A video world model performs the interacting operation of Definition 2.6 with video-centered state. Unlike general video generator, which aims at plausible content, it learns how that state evolves. We exclude models whose primary persistent state is an explicit 3D structure, such as neural field, 3D Gaussians, or an occupancy grid, as well as purely symbolic or text-based world models; models that keep 3D structure only as auxiliary memory for video-centered state remain in scope (Section 7.2.2). World models from model-based reinforcement learning are included only when their state is learned from video. We classify video world models along two independent axes. On the first axis, the prediction space, observationspace models predict future frames, video tokens, or generative latents decoded to video, as GAIA [172, 399] and EVA [71] do. Although VAE latents are not pixels, predicting them for decoding to video still counts as 14 Video Foundation Models World-Modeling Lens observation-space prediction. Latent-state models instead predict future video-derived features that need not be decoded to video: V-JEPA [20] and V-JEPA 2 [9] learn such features by masked feature prediction, which serves as pretraining for latent transition models (Section 7), and DINO-WM [652] and V-JEPA 2-AC add action-conditioned transitions for planning. The second axis, the transition interface, describes how controls reach the model. Passive models predict from observations alone, while action-conditioned models receive control sequence fixed before rollout, such as the ego trajectories of Vista [118] or the robot actions of IRASim [663]. Interactive models accept new controls during rollout, so each input can change what follows, as in GameNGen [459], Genie 2 [366], and related playable simulators [4, 32, 156, 631]. Section 7 reviews each cell of the resulting 2 3 grid (Figure 10).

sections.title: 4  Video Comprehension: Reading the World
sections.content: Reading means inferring world content, structure, dynamics, physics, and causality from partial video traces. Video comprehension performs the reading operation of Section 2: given trace , the model estimates properties of the latent world that produced it. From limited viewpoint and interval, it must recover which entities and events are present, where they are, how they change, which constraints govern that change, and what may have caused it. Occlusion, camera motion, editing, sparse sampling, and missing modalities leave much of this state unobserved, and the viewing scenarios of Section 3.1 change how much evidence must be selected and remembered. Sections 4.14.5 cover tasks and benchmarks, encoders, Video-LLMs, agents, and applications in turn. Tang et al. [438] survey Video-LLMs in more detail; here we organize the evaluation of reading by the world properties it tests (Section 4.1) and review Video-LLMs as one stage of the reading pipeline.

sections.title: 4.1 Tasks, Data, and Evaluation
sections.content: We organize video-understanding tasks by the main dimension of world state they require: semantic (entities, actions, events), spatial (location, identity, layout, viewpoint), temporal (order, duration, boundaries, long-range dependencies), physical (contact, gravity, containment, material behavior), and causal (effects, interventions, counterfactuals). The dimensions interact, as when tracking combines identity with temporal continuity, so Table 4 places each benchmark under the dimension it mainly tests, even when the text introduces it elsewhere. Output format is separate axis: label, span, mask, or sentence can probe any dimension, and what benchmark measures depends on the evidence needed to produce its output. Aggregate accuracy does not show that model used the intended evidence, since many questions can be answered from the text, single frame, or static appearance. Text-only, single-frame, shuffled-order, and restricted-context baselines expose these shortcuts, and TempCore [358] and Video-Index [420] use them to filter existing benchmarks down to vision-dependent, order-sensitive subsets. Minimal pairs of near-identical videos with different answers block appearance-only solutions (TimeBlind [235], MVP [222]).

sections.title: 4.1.1 Semantic Understanding
sections.content: Semantic understanding identifies the entities, actions, events, and relations that make video meaningful. Action recognition is the most established semantic task: UCF101 [424] and HMDB51 [225] test closed-set recognition in trimmed clips, Kinetics [208] scales up the number and diversity of classes, and SomethingSomething [132] makes labels depend on how objects change under manipulation. Language moves the output beyond fixed categories through retrieval (MSR-VTT [541]), captioning (VATEX [478], YouCook2 [655]), and video question answering (VideoQA: ActivityNet-QA [594], TVQA [234], TGIF-QA [199]). Recent Video-LLM benchmarks mix semantic questions with temporal, spatial, and knowledge-intensive items (Video-MME and Video-MME-v2 [109, 110], MMVU [643], Video-MMMU [177, 319]). Hallucination benchmarks test whether the reported content is supported by the video at all: VideoHallucer [322, 488] uses adversarially paired questions, EventHallusion [613] probes events suggested by language priors, and ARGUS [391] scores hallucination and omission in free-form captions. 15 Video Foundation Models World-Modeling Lens Table 4 Video-understanding benchmarks organized by the primary world-state property tested. benchmark may probe more than one dimension. sections.title: 4.1.2 Spatial Understanding
sections.content: Spatial understanding asks where entities are, how their extent changes, and whether their identity persists as viewpoint and visibility vary. Spatiotemporal grounding links referring expression to region tube over an interval (VidSTG [635]). Video object segmentation tracks pixel masks (DAVIS [373], YouTube-VOS [543]), referring variants select the target by language or motion (Ref-YouTube-VOS [404], MeViS [83]; addressed by ReferFormer [514]), and MOTChallenge [344] and LaSOT [94] test identity across occlusion and reappearance. Memory-based and promptable trackers such as XMem [67], AOT [571], DEVA [66], and SAM 2 [390] keep earlier evidence as the target changes appearance or disappears. Spatial reasoning benchmarks go beyond masks and tracks: VSI-Bench [559] and MMSI-Video-Bench [274] test relative position, viewpoint, and layout, STI-Bench [262] asks for quantitative pose and motion, and DSI-Bench [636] separates observer motion from object motion. newer group tests state that is out of view: SCP-Bench [642] infers unseen past or future layouts, Beyond3D [327] asks where relocated objects now are, and OVO-S-Bench [260] answers from the video prefix seen so far. These tasks test the object permanence and revisit consistency that world models must maintain (Section 7.2.2). 16 Video Foundation Models World-Modeling Lens

sections.title: 4.1.3 Temporal Understanding
sections.content: Temporal understanding recovers when an event occurs, how long it lasts, and how evidence at different moments is ordered or connected. Temporal action detection locates predefined actions in untrimmed video (THUMOS [195], ActivityNet [160]), and moment retrieval returns the segment that matches language query (Charades-STA [115], QVHighlights [233], DiDeMo [161]). Dense event captioning localizes and describes possibly overlapping events (ActivityNet Captions [221], addressed end to end by Vid2Seq [555]), and anticipation predicts an action not yet observed (e.g., Ego4D forecasting [133]). Fine-grained and long-form benchmarks stress subtle temporal differences and sparse evidence. TemporalBench [35] and TempCompass [303] test ordering, speed, and direction, TimeBlind [235] pairs videos that differ only in temporal structure, and Video-MME-Logical [227] separates logical complexity from scene recognition. MLVU [654], LVBench [472], and LongVideoBench [509] pose heterogeneous questions over long videos, and VideoOdyssey [151] extends this to ultra-long, omni-modal video, measuring how much context stays usable as evidence length grows. Streaming benchmarks make state maintenance directly observable. SVCBench [291] asks for running object and event counts at many points in video, TRACE [329] scores answer quality together with latency, false alarms, and missed responses under causal input, and StreamingEval [436] adds encoding throughput, time to first token, and fixed memory budget.

sections.title: 4.1.4 Physical Understanding
sections.content: Physical understanding concerns how visible state can change under constraints that are often only partly observed. Plausibility benchmarks ask whether an observed transition is possible: IntPhys [395] and IntPhys 2 [30] test object permanence and intuitive physics, ImplausiBench [345] contains videos that violate expected physical behavior, and Physion [23] instead asks whether objects will make contact. Other benchmarks ask for next states, interaction outcomes, or the mechanism behind change. CLEVRER [578] asks descriptive, predictive, and explanatory questions about collisions, while PhysicsMind [335], PhysBench [72], and PAI-Bench-U [651] broaden coverage to object properties, commonsense constraints, task completion, and next actions. APT [515] further labels timestamped transitions by mechanism (contact, gravity, or friction). Two benchmarks check that answers rest on physical evidence rather than priors. MVP [222] pairs nearidentical videos that require opposite answers, and VisPhyWorld [268] asks the model to rebuild the scene as executable simulator code so that its physical hypothesis can be checked. Physics benchmarks for generated video, such as Physics-IQ [346] and VideoPhy [16, 17], are covered in Sections 5.1.2 and 7.4.

sections.title: 4.1.5 Causal Understanding
sections.content: Causal understanding asks why an observed event occurred and how the outcome would change if an action, object, or condition were different. On synthetic collisions, CLEVRER [578] adds counterfactual questions to its explanatory ones. Real-world and procedural benchmarks link actions to effects that may appear much later: NExT-QA [526] and STAR [507] ask about event relations and reasons, Video-Holmes [68] and Causal2Needles [250] spread the clues far apart, and CaST-Bench [621] covers more varied settings and causal structures. Counterfactual benchmarks test altered outcomes directly: CausalVQA [108] asks counterfactual, hypothetical, and planning questions about real egocentric video, and DMC-CF [618] pairs such questions about real videos with causal-graph interventions, whose regenerated variants also limit data contamination.

sections.title: 4.2 Video Representation Learning and Encoding
sections.content: Video representation learning maps frames to features that can be reused across recognition, retrieval, grounding, reasoning, and multimodal modeling. Convolutional backbones such as I3D [39] and SlowFast [102] established supervised spatiotemporal processing, and TimeSformer [25], ViViT [8], and Video Swin [304] carried the Vision Transformer [86] to video at different spatial and temporal scales. The pretraining objective decides what these backbones retain, and we group objectives by their dominant supervision signal into the four families of Figure 3. The families overlap: masked feature prediction, for instance, is both masked and predictive. Variational autoencoders and tokenizers built for synthesis are covered in Section 5. 17 Video Foundation Models World-Modeling Lens Figure 3 Four families of video representation learning. They differ in how supervision targets are constructed and how predictions are compared with or generated from those targets.

sections.title: 4.2.1 Contrastive Learning
sections.content: Contrastive learning pulls positive pairs together in embedding space and pushes mismatched pairs apart, commonly with an InfoNCE-style objective. In video-only learning, CVRL [380] and ρMoCo [103] draw positives from augmentations or clips of the same video, and the sampling distance sets trade-off: views too close give little contrast, while views too far apart may show different events. Videotext contrastive learning pairs clips with language. Among dual-encoder retrieval models, Frozen in Time [14] trains spacetime Transformer jointly on imagetext and videotext pairs, and CLIP4Clip [316] transfers the CLIP imagetext encoder and adds temporal aggregation, while VideoCLIP [538], X-CLIP [330], ViCLIP [481], and Finsta [101] develop video-specific alignment. Foundation encoders combine contrastive pretraining with masked or generative losses (InternVideo [483], InternVideo2 [482]), distillation into maskedvideo student (VideoPrism [637]), or later alignment stages for language and dense prediction (Perception Encoder [29]). Global alignment can drop fine-grained detail: the World Embedding Benchmark [301] shows that alignment and recoverable physical state can diverge, as physics-specific contrastive tuning improves videotext matching but weakens physical-quantity regression from frozen features; the added losses aim to retain it.

sections.title: 4.2.2 Masked Learning
sections.content: Masked learning removes much of the spatiotemporal input and trains the model to recover it, an idea that VideoBERT [426] applied early to quantized video tokens and speech transcripts jointly. VideoMAE [453] reconstructs pixels behind tube masks, with high mask ratio that exploits the redundancy of adjacent frames, and VideoMAE-V2 [469] scales it with dual masking. Feature targets replace raw pixels: MaskFeat [497] reconstructs handcrafted or learned features, and UMT [249] distills from an unmasked teacher that sees the full clip. Learned or teacher targets shift capacity from low-level appearance toward the semantics and motion that the teacher encodes, but they also inherit its biases. 18 Video Foundation Models World-Modeling Lens

sections.title: 4.2.3 Predictive Learning
sections.content: Predictive learning trains model to predict the latent representation of hidden or future content, without pixel reconstruction or negative examples. V-JEPA [20] predicts the features of masked regions against slowly updated target encoder, V-JEPA 2 [9] scales this to larger and more diverse data, and V-JEPA 2.1 [348] improves dense features. InternVideo-Next [464] bridges the masked and predictive families, combining masked reconstruction with latent prediction of its first-stage targets, without videotext data. Adding an action-conditioned transition model to such representation yields the action-conditioned latent-state world models of Section 7.

sections.title: 4.2.4 Generative Learning
sections.content: Generative pretraining shapes representation by requiring it to produce missing or future content. Visual autoregressive objectives [553] predict future frames, patches, or tokens, which rewards sensitivity to appearance and motion but can spend capacity on reconstruction detail that recognition does not need. Vision-language generation outputs text instead: GIT-style [467] training generates captions or answers from visual features, and VideoCoCa [551] combines captioning with contrastive alignment. In both cases, the representation is shaped only by what captions describe. Large video diffusion models offer third route: Gen4U [213] reuses frozen generators intermediate activations for classification, geometry, and captioning, and GenCeption [468] adapts diffusion backbone into text-steered model for depth, normals, pose, segmentation, and keypoints (Section 6.2).

sections.title: 4.3 Video-Language Foundation Modeling
sections.content: Video-LLMs extend language foundation models to video for open-ended description, dialogue, question answering, grounding, and reasoning. They take visual features from encoders such as those in Section 4.2 and must decide which frames to observe, how to encode time, and how many visual tokens the language model can afford. We review their architectures, training, and test-time scaling in turn.

sections.title: 4.3.1 Architectures
sections.content: Visual front end. Many systems apply an image encoder such as CLIP [387] or SigLIP [455, 605] to sampled frames, route that is cheap and semantically strong but leaves temporal modeling to later modules. Nativevideo encoders [9, 662] model local motion before fusion, and direct patch or visual-token inputs keep finer spatial detail at higher context cost. No encoder can recover an event from an unsampled frame. Time and position. Frame order may be encoded by temporal embeddings, timestamps, or multidimensional rotary positions. Qwen2.5-VL [13] uses M-RoPE to coordinate temporal and spatial indices, Qwen3-VL [12] adds textual timestamps so that answers can cite moments, and the InternVL series [474] advances visual positions in fractional steps so that long sequences stay within the trained positional range. Temporal Transformers and state-space models such as Mamba [135] can also aggregate frame sequences before they reach the LLM. Vision-language connector. The connector maps visual features into the language backbones embedding space and token budget. Linear or MLP projectors turn each visual feature into prefix token, as in LLaVA-style systems [282], while Q-Former and resampler designs [246] extract fixed number of query tokens, as in early Video-LLaMA [610] and VideoChat [247]. Gated cross-attention, as in Flamingo [2], instead lets language layers consult visual features at selected depths. Structure-preserving compressors downsample while keeping spatial layout, through convolutional abstractors (Honeybee [40]), spatial-temporal convolution (VideoLLaMA 2 [70]), or pixel unshuffle (InternVL [474]). Projectors keep the most direct token path, resamplers and cross-attention give the most control over how much visual information enters the LLM, and compressors trade some directness for locality-aware reduction. Compression and memory. Video token count grows with both the number of frames and the tokens per frame, and pooling, merging, or resampling reduce it at the risk of erasing small objects, short events, or precise timestamps. sections.title: 4.3.2 Learning Paradigms
sections.content: Video-LLMs are usually trained in stages because the encoder, connector, and language backbone start from different representations. In alignment pretraining, the encoder and LLM are often frozen while the connector learns from caption pairs, videotext matching, and grounding data, following the visual instruction tuning recipe for images [282]. Table 6 lists pair corpora and instruction datasets for this stage and the next. Supervised instruction tuning. Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) then trains on VideoQA and dialogue data for question-conditioned answers, temporal grounding data for timestamps [379], and spatial grounding 21 Video Foundation Models World-Modeling Lens data for coordinates or other structured outputs. Which components are updated varies: early VideoChatGPT [332] tunes only its projector, Video-LLaVA [271] also updates the LLM, and VideoLLaMA3 [606] and VideoChat3 [256] adapt both the visual and language components  (Table 5)  . The mixture of image, short-video, long-video, optical character recognition (OCR), and grounding data decides whether model mainly describes clips or can locate and reason over the evidence behind an answer. Preference optimization and reinforcement learning. Post-training can then optimize preferences or task outcomes. Reinforcement learning (RL) from human feedback [361] and direct preference optimization, which Qwen2.5-VL [13] and VistaDPO [183] apply after SFT, improve visual faithfulness only insofar as the feedback separates grounded content from fluent but unsupported answers. Reasoning-oriented methods instead use verifiable rewards, often with group relative policy optimization (GRPO) [138]. Video-R1 [105] adds temporal reward that compares rollouts on ordered and shuffled frames, LongVILA-R1 [63] scales RL to long videos through its data and distributed training, and OneThinker [106] broadens the task mixture and normalizes advantages with running per-task reward statistics. Task-specific rewards target the output directly: Time-R1 [480] rewards timestamp intersection-over-union for temporal grounding, VideoChat-R1 [255] jointly rewards spatiotemporal tasks without hurting general QA, and VideoP2R [202] rewards perception and reasoning separately. Others modify GRPO itself: DeepVideo-R1 [365] recasts it as advantage regression with difficulty-aware augmentation, and GRPO-CARE [62] adds bonus if slowly updated reference model reproduces the answer from the reasoning trace. Data and scaling. Data and curriculum matter as much as model size. Current recipes such as InternVideo3 [554], Qwen3-VL [12], and VideoLLaMA3 [606] train jointly on image, video, and language data and widen task coverage with synthetic instructions; InternVideo3 and Qwen3-VL also add long-context curricula and use on-policy distillation to supply responses from states the model actually visits. Apollo [667] studies this design space systematically, measuring how frame sampling, encoder choice, and token allocation interact across model scales. Newer corpora add finer temporal supervision: OneStreamer-1M [603] times its captions and QA to the evidence available at each response point.

sections.title: 4.3.3 Test-Time Scaling
sections.content: Test-time scaling spends extra computation after training to read the available video better. Multimodal chainof-thought [100, 318] spends tokens on intermediate reasoning, which helps only if those steps stay grounded in the frames. Query-aware frame selection instead spends compute on choosing the input: SeViLA [591] and VideoTree [494] rank, retain, or hierarchically organize frames for the query. Iterative thinking with video methods such as FrameThinker [159] and VideoChat-A1 [493] alternate between reasoning and revisiting frames over several steps. Search and aggregation select among several reasoning paths by self-consistency, best-of-N , or verifier and process-reward models, while V-Reason [425] directly modifies the models inference-time behavior instead of sampling more outputs. Each route trades latency and repeated visual computation for broader exploration or second look at ambiguous evidence. The boundary with agentic modeling is gradual: thinking-with-video methods already revisit frames, and once model issues explicit operations to fetch new crops, frames, retrieval results, or persistent memory, it enters the agentic setting of Section 4.4.

sections.title: 4.4 Agentic Video Modeling
sections.content: Agentic video modeling turns evidence acquisition into sequential decision problem: an LLM or Video-LLM forms subquestions, chooses temporal region or visual detail to inspect, invokes an operation, and updates its reasoning from the result until it can answer. Its actions change access to the recording by locating segments, sampling frames, cropping regions, querying tracks, or retrieving memory; actions that change the depicted world belong to the interactive rollouts of Section 7.

Beyond answer accuracy, evaluation should report whether the retrieved evidence supports the answer and what the search costs; REPAIR [3] adds repeated paired runs to separate run-to-run variance from method effects and counts the operations and latency hidden behind visible tool calls.

sections.title: 4.4.2 Tool Use and Retrieval Augmentation
sections.content: Tools supply observations that the base model cannot obtain reliably from its current context: detectors and trackers for entity state, temporal grounders for event boundaries, croppers for spatial detail, and OCR, speech recognition, or captioners for other modalities. In modular agents, prompted controller composes external tools: VisProg [142] and ViperGPT [431] generate executable programs over vision tools without training. Native tool-calling models instead learn when to call tool, with which parameters, and how to use the result. LongVT [572] surveys long video, predicts relevant interval, and crops and densely resamples it before continuing to reason, and VideoThinker [239] learns temporal retrieval and zoom from tool trajectories synthesized in caption space and grounded back to video. Ego-R1 [448] trains chain of tool-thought with RL over dayand week-long egocentric recordings. Tool use can also be distilled away: Agent-of-Thoughts 24 Video Foundation Models World-Modeling Lens Distillation [414] distills agent traces into single Video-LLM as chain-of-thought supervision, trading flexibility for one-pass inference. Retrieval augmentation moves evidence into an external index. One VideoRAG [200] retrieves query-relevant videos and keeps both their visual and textual content, while another [394] combines graph-based text grounding with multimodal encoding to search very large collections. The retrieval unit shapes what can be recovered: fixed-length chunks may split an event, so SceneRAG [602] indexes narrative scenes and adds an entity-relation graph for multi-hop retrieval, at the cost of errors in segmentation and graph construction. Tools and retrieval address different bottlenecks: cropper or grounder fetches finer local evidence on demand, whereas an index narrows the search across long videos or corpora. Both still require the system to decide what to request, detect missing or conflicting evidence, and trace the answer back to its source clips.

sections.title: 4.5 Applications
sections.content: Applications pose these problems under domain-specific viewpoints, vocabularies, and event structures.

sections.title: 4.5.1 Embodied and Egocentric Perception
sections.content: Egocentric video records activity from the wearers viewpoint, so the camera moves with the body, hands occlude manipulated objects, and key events are separated by long stretches of routine activity. Standard resources include EPIC-KITCHENS-100 [78], Ego4D [133], EgoSchema [336], and the paired firstand third-person views of Ego-Exo4D [134] (Section 3.1). An egocentric assistant has to track the manipulated object and its state, the current task step, and the earlier event that explains the present situation, even when the object is hidden behind the hand or out of view. Newer benchmarks target specific settings. EgoTools [447] tests understanding of physical tools and their effects (not software-tool calls), covering affordance, grounding, procedure, and spatial reasoning, and EgoPolice [129] tests police body-worn camera footage, where consequential events are rare and visibility is poor.

sections.title: 4.5.2 Autonomous Driving
sections.content: Driving video must be read as dynamic scene of road geometry, traffic controls, vehicles, pedestrians, and their relations. BDD100K [584] supplies diverse annotated road video, and nuScenes [33] and the Waymo Open Dataset [428] add synchronized camera and range-sensor sequences with 3D annotations. Languagebased benchmarks ask which participants and relations matter: DriveLM [416] links key objects and their interactions to prediction and planning questions through graph-structured VideoQA, and the frame-level NuScenes-SpatialQA [445] tests spatial relations in driving scenes. OmniDrive [471] aligns language reasoning with 3D driving tasks and adds counterfactual questions about how alternative actions would change an outcome. The resulting scene state links video reading to the trajectory prediction, action selection, and closed-loop control of Section 7.

sections.title: 4.5.3 Domain-Specific Video Analysis
sections.content: Medical and surgical video. Surgical video is structured by procedure phases, so recognizing visible instruments is not enough. EndoNet [456] introduced Cholec80 for phase and tool recognition, CholecT50 and Rendezvous [356] refine the output into instrumentverbtarget triplets, and SurgVLM [604] combines perception, temporal analysis, and question answering across surgical tasks. Evaluation must check phase, anatomy, and action against the structured labels of clinical workflows, not the fluency of description. Sports analytics. match contains long stretches of routine play broken by brief, rule-dependent events. SoccerNet [127] defined action spotting in broadcast soccer; SoccerNet-v2 [80] adds camera-shot segmentation and replay grounding, which require precise localization and knowledge of broadcast structure. Film and edited video. In edited footage, shot size, cut type, and transitions are deliberate choices. VEUBench [237] tests recognition, reasoning, and judging of editing attributes within and across shots, and finds that general Video-LLMs handle them poorly, in some cases below chance. 25 Video Foundation Models World-Modeling Lens Education and instructional video. Instructional video follows procedure from an initial state through intermediate steps to goal. HowTo100M [343] supplies narrated demonstrations, and CrossTask [666] and COIN [437] annotate steps for temporal localization. Reading such video means tracking the progress of the procedure: separating narrated intention from visible operation, recovering omitted or repeated steps, and reasoning about order and prerequisites. INSIGHT Video understanding is limited by state, not by context length Encoders compress observations, Video-LLMs map evidence into language, and agents choose what to inspect, but all of them are limited by what state they keep and ground, not by how many frames they accept. Longer context helps only when it corrects or stabilizes that state, so evaluation should ask whether added evidence improves the state estimate, stays traceable to source clips, and survives later queries. 5 (cid:210) Video Generation: Writing the World Writing means rendering new video trace from partial world specification supplied as text, images, audio, motion, or other conditions. Video generation is the writing operation of Section 2: its conditions fix some entities, relations, and dynamics of and leave the rest to the generator. Text may specify an event, an image may fix its initial appearance, audio may set visible rhythm or articulation, and trajectories camera or object motion. This chapter covers models whose output and training target are the video itself, judged by fidelity, condition adherence, temporal coherence, and controllable revision. Persistent state under occlusion, revisits, long rollouts, and actions is treated in Section 7. We cover tasks and evaluation, latent representations, generative paradigms, control strategies, and applications. Xing et al. [535] review video diffusion models in depth.

sections.title: 5.1 Tasks, Conditions, and Evaluation
sections.content: A video-generation task is defined by the information fixed before synthesis: text, images, source videos, audio, reference identities, or prescribed motion. Evaluation measures the visual and temporal quality of the result, its adherence to the condition, and the stability of the entities, events, and physical relations it shows. Table 9 lists training resources, Table 10 lists metrics and learned scorers, and Table 11 lists benchmarks and the conditions they test.

sections.title: 5.1.1 Generation Tasks by Condition
sections.content: Text, image, and video conditions. Text-to-video (T2V) maps description of content, style, or events to video and leaves most appearance and motion to the model, as in Sora [31], Wan [462], and HunyuanVideo [219]. Image-to-video (I2V) fixes the initial state or reference appearance and must add plausible motion without losing that structure and identity, as in Stable Video Diffusion [27] and the human-animation systems Animate Anyone [179] and MagicAnimate [548]. Video-to-video (V2V) starts from source video and covers transformations with different preservation requirements. Editing changes selected content and should stay local, as in Tune-A-Video [512], Video-P2P [293], FateZero [377], and TokenFlow [126]. Translation maps the source to another appearance or domain while keeping its content. Interpolation connects observed endpoints, and extension continues the sequence beyond its last frame, as in NUWA-XL [580], SEINE [60], and StreamingT2V [162]. Audio and audio-visual conditions. In audio-driven generation, speech, music, or sound track sets visible dynamics such as lip motion, expression, gesture, or rhythm, as in Wav2Lip [375], SadTalker [626], EMO [446], and Hallo [542]. Joint audio-video generation instead produces both streams and must keep their events synchronized as well as each stream plausible, as in JavisDiT [288], JavisDiT++ [289], and Ovi [309]. Geometric, motion, and identity conditions. Camera, motion, and trajectory conditions prescribe how the viewpoint or scene elements evolve. Camera poses and paths control the observation process, as in 26 Video Foundation Models World-Modeling Lens CameraCtrl [152], while object trajectories, human poses, and action sequences constrain motion within the scene, as in MotionCtrl [492], DragNUWA [579], VideoComposer [475], and Wan-Move [73]. Identityor subject-conditioned generation, as in ConsisID [597], fixes which person, object, or subject persists over time, and that subject must stay stable under pose, viewpoint, and occlusion changes. Any-conditioned and unified control. Any-conditioned systems accept variable subset of text, image, audio, structure, motion, and reference inputs, as in FullDiT [207], UNIC [576], and Any2Caption [517]. They must bind each cue to the right entity, region, time span, or modality and reconcile cues of different granularity. Section 5.4 describes how such conditions enter the model. Training supervision. Each task needs training pairs that expose its conditionoutput correspondence  (Table 9)  . Caption corpora such as Panda-70M [56] and UltraVideo [550] serve T2V, and image conditioning and extension can be learned by keeping selected frames or prefixes of clip [203]. Editing needs sourceinstructiontarget triplets, as in OpenVE-3M [153]. Camera control uses posed video such as RealEstate10K [657], motion control uses tracked point trajectories [73], and audio-visual generation needs synchronized tracks such as VGGSound [50]. Identity control pairs references and targets from different contexts or shots, as in Phantom-Data [65], MuSS [611], and Omni-R2V [253], so the model cannot simply copy the references pose or background into the output.

sections.title: 5.1.2 Evaluation and Metrics
sections.content: Video-generation quality has several dimensions, and the right profile depends on the task: T2V emphasizes semantic alignment, editing requires source preservation and locality, audio-driven generation requires synchronization, and motion control requires trajectory adherence. single aggregate score hides the failure that limits system, so we group metrics by the property they measure  (Table 10)  and benchmarks by the cases they test  (Table 11)  . Visual fidelity and temporal quality. FID [165] compares frame-feature distributions and ignores temporal order. The Inception Score [401] rewards confident, diverse classifier predictions without reference to real data, which limits its meaning outside the classifiers domain [21]. FVD [457] extends the comparison to video features, but it depends on the feature extractor and sample count and can under-penalize temporal corruption in favor of static samples [121]. JEDi [314] instead uses V-JEPA features and maximum mean discrepancy, avoiding FVDs Gaussian assumption and needing fewer samples. PSNR, SSIM [491], and LPIPS [623] suit reconstruction and source preservation but penalize valid alternative futures. FVMD [283] and STREAM [212] target motion consistency and spatiotemporal quality, and VMBench [279] checks whether motion strength matches the prompt. Diversity needs repeated samples under one condition: DiVid [175] measures variation in semantics, style, subject, scene, motion, and camera alongside quality and faithfulness. Condition alignment and compositionality. Condition-aware evaluation checks whether the video follows its condition. CLIPScore [164] measures imagecaption similarity, and its frame-averaged video variants ignore temporal order and motion. cFreD [220] adds textvisual cross-covariances to conditional Fréchet distance, so it penalizes videos swapped among prompts, which marginal distance cannot detect. FETV [302] and T2V-CompBench [427] separate objects, attributes, relations, actions, and temporal composition. Structured conditions have their own tests: MultiRef-Compass [628] checks how several references bind to audiovisual content. OmniVBench [253] applies case-specific checklists for reference fidelity and binding, and MoveBench [73] measures trajectory endpoint error. For source-conditioned tasks, V2V-Bench [295] scores what the instruction should change separately from what the source should preserve. Physical and world consistency. Realistic local motion can still show impossible interactions, unstable objects, or broken persistence. VideoPhy [16] and VideoPhy-2 [17] test physical commonsense, the latter in harder action-centric interactions. PhysicsMind [335] and VideoScience-Bench [178] test mechanics and basic scientific phenomena, and PhyAVBench [532] tests whether generated sound changes with paired physical conditions. PhyProbe [223] instead trains physical-violation scorer on frozen visual features and shows that prior learned evaluators depend on their annotation distributions, though it retains some dataset dependence itself. Persistence under revisits and occlusion is tested by the world-model benchmarks of Section 7.4. Human preference, learned evaluators, and suites. Human comparisons capture coherence, visual appeal, and instruction adherence that fixed feature distances miss. sections.title: 5.2 Video Latent Representation Learning
sections.content: Many current video generators work in compressed latent space: an encoder maps video to shorter representation, the generator models its distribution, and decoder reconstructs the frames. Compression lowers training and sampling cost, especially for long videos, while the bottleneck and decoder decide whether fine texture, fast motion, and small objects survive. Figure 4 contrasts the four families: continuous latents for diffusion and flow objectives, discrete tokens for autoregressive or masked prediction, hybrids that mix continuous and discrete forms or pair tokenizer with diffusion decoder, and semantically aligned representations that also serve understanding.

sections.title: 5.2.1 Continuous Latents
sections.content: Per-frame image VAEs. Latent diffusion [396] established the value of training generative model in the continuous space of pretrained image autoencoder, and the simplest video extension encodes each frame independently. VideoLDM [28] and AnimateDiff [141] reuse image autoencoders and add temporal layers to image diffusion backbones. This keeps the image prior and eases reuse of text-to-image backbones. However, the latent sequence still grows linearly with the number of frames, and temporal coherence must be learned by the generator or by temporal layers in the decoder. 29 Video Foundation Models World-Modeling Lens Table 11 Benchmarks for conditioned video and audio-video generation and editing. Video VAEs use 3D or factorized spatiotemporal operations to compress both resolution and time. Temporal compression shortens the sequence, lowers attention cost, and exploits redundancy between nearby frames, but an aggressive bottleneck can smooth brief events or fast motion. CV-VAE [641] keeps its video latent space compatible with pretrained image VAE so that image-generation priors remain usable, whereas CogVideoX [570] and Cosmos [355] use dedicated 3D tokenizers for high spatial and temporal compression. causal 3D VAE computes the latent at time without future frames and encodes the first frame without preceding context, so one tokenizer handles both images and videos and streaming or autoregressive generators see no future leakage. 30 Video Foundation Models World-Modeling Lens Figure 4 Latent representations for video generation. Continuous, discrete, hybrid, and semantically aligned designs differ in how tokenizers and VAEs shape reconstruction fidelity, compression, sequence modeling, and unification with understanding. Semantic alignment can be applied to either continuous or discrete representations.

sections.title: 5.2.2 Discrete Tokens
sections.content: From vector quantization to codebook-free schemes. VQ-VAE [359] replaces each encoder output with the index of learned codebook entry, producing categorical symbols that next-token or masked-token models can predict. VQGAN [93] improves high-resolution reconstruction with perceptual and adversarial losses, and RQ-VAE [231] stacks residual codes to increase precision without enlarging the token grid. Learned codebooks, however, may be used unevenly or collapse to small active subset. Later quantizers drop the learned codebook: FSQ [342] rounds few scalar dimensions to fixed levels, LFQ in MAGVIT-v2 [589] uses binary dimensions to obtain very large implicit vocabulary, and BSQ [644] projects embeddings onto hypersphere before binary quantization. They differ in optimization stability, vocabulary size, and distortion at given token budget. Video tokenization. The video encoder also fixes the spatiotemporal extent of each token and hence the sequence length. C-ViViT in Phenaki [461] factorizes spatial and temporal encoding into causal discrete tokens, MAGVIT-v2 pairs causal tokenizer with LFQ for both autoregressive and masked generation, and HiTVideo [661] shortens the sequence with hierarchical codes that place semantics and fine detail in different layers. Fixed grids, however, spend as many tokens on static shot as on fast-changing scene. Adaptive tokenizers allocate the budget by content: EVATok [536] predicts how many tokens each segment needs, and VideoFlexTok [10] emits variable-length coarse-to-fine sequence whose early tokens carry semantics and motion and whose later tokens add detail.

sections.title: 5.2.3 Hybrid and Semantically Aligned Representations
sections.content: Hybrid tokenizers combine continuous and discrete forms or change the decoder. OneVAE [660] initializes discrete video VAE from continuous one and trains both in one network, so continuous latents can feed diffusion or flow models and discrete codes can feed sequence models. Divot [122] and DiCoDe [261] 31 Video Foundation Models World-Modeling Lens Figure 5 Generative modeling paradigms. Diffusion and flow matching learn denoising or velocity targets over video latents. Autoregressive modeling factorizes an ordered sequence, while masked prediction fills selected positions from visible context through parallel conditional predictions. instead decode with diffusion model. Divot learns continuous features for LLM-based understanding and reconstruction, and DiCoDe compresses video into deep tokens that an LLM predicts autoregressively. Semantic alignment adds further requirement. reconstruction-optimal latent may keep texture and local motion without organizing them into the objects, events, and relations needed for understanding, while highly semantic latent may discard the detail that generation needs. VILA-U [521] trains one discrete tokenizer for both reconstruction and text alignment, and the SEED tokenizer [123] gives language model semantically organized visual code. PyraTok [432] quantizes features at several spatiotemporal scales against one text-guided codebook, so coarse semantics and fine detail occupy different levels. Section 6 pursues this question in models that share LLMs, parameters, or objectives across understanding and generation. Representation autoencoders start from the semantic side: they freeze pretrained encoder as the tokenizer and train only projector or pooler and decoder. V-RAE [139] compares image and video encoders such as DINOv3 and V-JEPA 2.1 and finds that reconstruction ranking does not consistently predict generation quality, so semantic latent must be tested inside the target generator.

sections.title: 5.3 Generative Video Foundation Modeling
sections.content: Video generators differ in their generative objective, the order in which space-time units are predicted, and the system that organizes synthesis. Diffusion, autoregressive or masked prediction, and flow matching define model-level generation processes (Figure 5), whereas LLM/MLLM-assisted and agentic systems add planning, tool use, and revision around visual generator that may use any of the three. The levels combine in practice: system may denoise each chunk while rolling out autoregressively in time, and an agent may repeatedly call flow-based generator. Preference optimization is applied on top of these generators. VideoReward [284] aligns flow-based generator with Flow-DPO on multidimensional preference signal, and LiFT [484] applies reward-weighted fine-tuning with reward model learned from human annotations. World-R1 [473] uses feedback from pretrained 3D and vision-language models to reinforce geometric consistency through Flow-GRPO. sections.title: 5.3.1 Diffusion-Based Generation
sections.content: Diffusion models learn to reverse gradual corruption process: clean video latent is perturbed according to noise schedule, and the model learns to predict the noise, velocity, or an equivalent denoising target at any noise level [167, 396]. The ϵand v-prediction objectives and EDM-style schedules are alternative parameterizations of this problem (Section 3.3); they affect optimization and sampling, not the video architecture. Flow-matching generators (Section 5.3.3) share these backbones, so the backbone and long-video designs below apply to both. Backbone and attention. Early video diffusion systems, including Video Diffusion Models [169], Imagen Video [166], and Make-A-Video [417], extended convolutional U-Nets with temporal convolutions or factorized spatial and temporal attention. Lumiere [19] instead generates the whole clip in one pass with spacetime U-Net that downsamples in both space and time, avoiding keyframe generation followed by temporal 34 Video Foundation Models World-Modeling Lens super-resolution. Diffusion Transformers (DiTs) [369] then made it easier to scale attention over compressed space-time tokens. CogVideoX [570], Mochi [125], and LTX-Video [145] pair causal or highly compressed video VAE with DiT. CogVideoX uses an expert Transformer with separate text and video normalization, Mochi gives the visual stream more capacity in an asymmetric DiT, and LTX-Video compresses aggressively so that full spatiotemporal attention stays affordable. Joint audio-video backbones couple two modality streams through bidirectional cross-modal attention, so timing and semantics are exchanged throughout synthesis. LTX-2 [144] extends LTX-Video with separate modality VAEs and asymmetric audio and video streams, and Ovi [309] couples matched audio and video DiTs trained with flow matching. The main backbone trade-off concerns attention. Factorized attention separates spatial and temporal interactions to save cost, whereas full spatiotemporal attention lets all space-time tokens interact at higher memory cost. Sparse and linear attention cut this cost for long or high-resolution clips. HunyuanVideo 1.5 [506] uses selective and sliding tile attention within unified T2V and I2V training framework, and SANA-Video 2.0 [53] interleaves gated linear attention with periodic softmax layers and routes block summaries across depth. Conditions enter the backbone through cross-attention, adaptive normalization such as AdaLN, joint text-video attention, or channel and token concatenation (Section 5.4). Streaming and long videos. Standard diffusion denoises fixed-length clip as whole, whereas streaming variants generate causally, chunk by chunk. Diffusion Forcing [44] gives each frame its own noise level, MAGI-1 [443] denoises chunks autoregressively, CausVid [582] distills bidirectional model into few-step causal generator, Self-Forcing [190] trains on the models own rollouts, and Causal Forcing [664] distills from an autoregressive teacher (Section 7.2.2, Table 17). S2PD [176] instead changes the sampling order within clip, generating blocks autoregressively at high noise, then refining the sequence in parallel at low noise. Long videos raise different problem: repeated local generation keeps short-term motion but gradually loses appearance and global structure. StreamingT2V [162] carries anchor frames and shortand long-term memory across windows, FreeLong [313] blends low-frequency global features with high-frequency local ones during denoising without training, and FramePack [619] compresses past frames by importance to bound the context. Other methods change training or the history representation. LongTake [364] supervises later frames from long real-video prefixes before self-rollout distribution matching, and its evaluation separates sustained motion from appearance quality, since nearly static continuation can score well on consistency. Test-time training [77] stores context in MLP weights that self-supervised loss updates while the sequence is processed, and has been demonstrated on one-minute, storyboard-conditioned cartoons.

sections.title: 5.3.2 Autoregressive and Masked Token Generation
sections.content: Autoregressive video models factorize the distribution over an ordered sequence of video units. With discrete tokens, this resembles language modeling: VideoGPT [553] paired VQ-VAE with Transformer prior over video codes, CogVideo [170] scaled the recipe to text-conditioned generation, and VideoPoet [217] applied it in multimodal sequence model. Loong [487] places text and video tokens in one sequence and uses short-to-long training and inference-time re-encoding to limit error accumulation in minute-level videos. InfinityStar [285] extends discrete autoregression to 720p image, video, and long-video generation, reporting about 30 times lower latency than Wan 2.1-14B in its own single-GPU setting. The route offers standard causal likelihood and flexible length, at the cost of long decoding chains, dependence on tokenizer quality, and errors that propagate through the prefix. Masked generation relaxes the one-token-at-a-time order: the model predicts sets of masked positions from visible tokens, often refining coarse-to-fine over several rounds. Phenaki [461] applies bidirectional masked Transformer to causal video tokens, MAGVIT-v2 [589] improves the tokenizer and the masked generation framework, and Lumos-1 [595] keeps frames causal while decoding each frame in parallel with mask-based discrete diffusion. Continuous tokens support the same factorization. MAR [252] introduced diffusion loss for the conditional distribution of continuous image token, and NOVA [82] and VideoMAR [585] carry it to video, predicting frames causally in time and continuous tokens within each frame with diffusion loss. 35 Video Foundation Models World-Modeling Lens Figure 6 System-level organization for video generation. An LLM or MLLM plans for visual generator through an explicit plan, such as shot lists, storyboards, or layouts, or through learned plan embeddings, and agentic systems close the loop with scripting, generation, evaluation, and revision under controller.

sections.title: 5.3.3 Flow-Based Generation
sections.content: Flow matching [280] trains time-dependent vector field that transports samples from simple base distribution to the data along prescribed probability path, and generation integrates the corresponding ordinary differential equation. It differs from the usual diffusion account in its training target and sampling path: rectified-flow formulations favor nearly straight paths, which can reduce the number of solver steps, and the same DiT or multimodal DiT (MMDiT) can parameterize either target. Stable Diffusion 3 [92] made the rectified-flow and MMDiT combination prominent for images, and video systems adapted it to space-time latents. HunyuanVideo [219], Step-Video-T2V [328], Goku [55], and Wan [462] scale flow matching with DiT backbones and video VAEs, HunyuanVideo with dual-stream-to-single-stream Transformer. Pyramid Flow [205] changes the path itself, linking spatial pyramid stages and compressing full-resolution history with temporal pyramid so that one DiT is trained end to end across resolutions. Normalizing flows are distinct, likelihood-based route that should not be confused with flow matching. STARFlow-V [136] applies invertible autoregressive transformations to pretrained video-VAE latents, with globallocal decomposition and light causal denoiser, so the likelihood is tractable in latent space.

sections.title: 5.3.4 LLM/MLLM-Assisted Generation
sections.content: LLM/MLLM-assisted generation covers systems in which language model plans, expands, captions, or structures the conditions for separate visual sampler. language model that predicts video tokens directly belongs to autoregressive generation instead. In the common arrangement (Figure 6), the language model turns an underspecified request into scenes, shots, layouts, or refined prompts that diffusion, flow, or autoregressive generator consumes. VideoDirectorGPT [273] produces grounded video plan before layout-conditioned generation, and LLM-grounded Video Diffusion [265] and Dysen-VDM [99] draft dynamic scene layouts or scene graphs that guide the denoiser, so the language model handles composition and timing while the video model handles appearance and motion. Any2Caption [517] interprets text, image, video, region, motion, and camera cues and translates them into dense structured captions for downstream generator. The language model and the generator can also be coupled more tightly than through written prompt. MetaCanvas [272] lets an MLLM plan in spatial or spatiotemporal latent spaces connected to diffusion backbones, including image-to-video and editing settings. TV2TV [148] couples the two more tightly, interleaving language next-token prediction with video flow matching in one framework.

sections.title: 5.3.5 Agentic Generation
sections.content: Agentic generation turns planning into an executable loop: controller decomposes request, calls specialized models or tools, inspects intermediate results, and revises the plan or conditions when the output falls short (Figure 6). The recurring stages are scripting, storyboarding, visual generation, evaluation, and revision. 36 Video Foundation Models World-Modeling Lens Figure 7 Control mechanisms by intervention site. Each route is identified by the component through which its principal control signal enters generation: the input, the attention maps, the latent state, block features, parameters and embeddings, or the sampling update. Current agents mainly decompose long-form creation or coordinate tools. MovieAgent [519] assigns screenplay, directing, storyboard, and scene construction to cooperating agents, and Anim-Director [263] has an MLLM write storyline and script, produce consistent scene references, and select outputs from generative tools. Mora [599] routes among generation and editing skills in multi-agent workflow.

sections.title: 5.4 Control Strategies
sections.content: Section 5.1 classifies generation by the information supplied; here we classify control by the component through which that information alters generation. camera path, pose sequence, or reference image may enter as input tokens, adapter features, latent trajectory, sampling guidance, or tuned parameters. This entry point determines what must be trained, how strong and local the control is, and how easily several signals combine. Figure 7 locates the entry points relative to the backbone, and Table 13 compares the six families. single system often combines several, as in source inversion followed by attention reuse and classifier-free guidance.

sections.title: 5.4.1 Attention-Based Control
sections.content: Attention-based methods reuse the correspondences that text-conditioned generator already forms: crossattention links prompt tokens to spatial features, and self-attention relates visual features to one another. Prompt-to-Prompt [163] injects cross-attention maps from source prompt into the denoising run for an edited prompt, keeping the layout while changing word, an attribute, or concepts strength. Video editing also needs the change to stay stable across frames. Video-P2P [293] and FateZero [377] combine attention control with inversion of the source video. Video-P2P adds separate guidance for source and target prompts, and FateZero fuses source and target crossand self-attention maps recorded during inversion. TokenFlow [126] instead propagates diffusion features between frames through feature-space correspondences, 37 Video Foundation Models World-Modeling Lens Table 13 Control strategies for video generation, grouped by where the control signal enters the generator (Figure 7).
