sections.title: 5.4.2 Adapter-Based Control
sections.content: Adapters add trainable path for external structure while keeping most or all of the pretrained generator frozen. ControlNet [620] copies the encoder blocks of frozen image diffusion model into conditional branch joined by zero-initialized convolutions, whereas T2I-Adapter [347] adds features from small condition encoder at several resolutions. They represent the two main variants: heavy side network that mirrors the backbone 38 Video Foundation Models World-Modeling Lens and light adapter that produces residual features. Video adapters must also encode how condition changes over time. MotionCtrl [492] represents camera motion with poses and object motion with trajectories so that the two can be composed. VideoControlNet [182] brings ControlNet to video-to-video translation with motion guidance that keeps the injected structure aligned across frames. Unified adapters train several controls together. VACE [203] encodes reference frames, source video, and masks in Video Condition Unit and injects them into frozen DiT through context adapter, supporting reference generation, editing, and masked editing with shared adapter parameters.

sections.title: 5.4.3 Latent-Space Control
sections.content: Latent-space methods act on the noisy sample or the denoising trajectory itself. Partial noising, as in SDEdit [340], perturbs an input to an intermediate noise level and denoises it under new condition, so the noise level trades fidelity against edit strength. Inversion maps an observed video to noise trajectory from which the generator approximately reconstructs it, often through deterministic DDIM sampling [421]; editing then changes the condition or selected latents along the reverse path. method may also construct latent conditions directly. Wan-Move [73] projects dense point trajectories into latent space and propagates first-frame features along them, giving an image-to-video model motion condition without separate motion encoder. VLIPP [564] has vision-language model plan coarse object motion, renders the plan as synthetic motion video, and converts its optical flow into structured noise that initializes motion-controllable image-to-video model (Section 7.2.4).

sections.title: 5.4.4 Concatenation and In-Context Conditioning
sections.content: The most direct route places the condition in the model input. Channel concatenation appends aligned condition latents to the noisy video latent, as in the image-to-video variants of Stable Video Diffusion [27] and CogVideoX [570] and in VideoComposer [475], which fuses spatial and temporal conditions before concatenation. Token concatenation instead appends condition embeddings to the sequence processed by selfor joint attention. FullDiT [207] maps heterogeneous conditions into one sequence and models them with full attention, avoiding separately trained side branches. In-context generation places reference examples or sourcetarget pairs in the sequence so that the model infers the requested transformation, as Emu2 [429] showed for multimodal image generation and UNIC [576] applies to unified video editing. Retrieval can supply further condition tokens: PhysRAG [69] retrieves videos of relevant physical phenomena, extracts physical information, and injects it into video diffusion model through learnable queries.

sections.title: 5.4.5 Guidance-Based Control
sections.content: Guidance changes the sampling direction instead of adding persistent condition branch. Classifier-free guidance (CFG) [168] combines conditional and unconditional predictions at each denoising step, (cid:98)ϵcfg = ϵθ(zk, k, ) + γ(cid:0)ϵθ(zk, k, c) ϵθ(zk, k, )(cid:1), where zk is the noisy latent at denoising step k, denotes the null condition, and γ is the guidance scale; γ = 1 recovers the conditional prediction. CFG needs model trained with condition dropout, and raising γ usually strengthens alignment but reduces diversity. (6) More general guidance uses the gradient of an energy, attention, correspondence, or physical objective to modify each update and can impose constraints absent from the training data. Universal guidance [15] and training-free energy guidance [588] use external objectives, whereas diffusion self-guidance [91] defines them on the generators internal attention and feature maps.

sections.title: 5.4.6 Tuning-Based Control
sections.content: Tuning stores new subject, style, or source-video prior in learned embeddings or weights. For images, Textual Inversion [112] learns new text embeddings for user concept, DreamBooth [398] fine-tunes the model on 39 Video Foundation Models World-Modeling Lens few subject images with prior-preservation loss, and LoRA [174] learns low-rank weight updates while keeping the base weights fixed. Video adds the requirement that the learned identity stay stable under motion and viewpoint change. Tune-A-Video [512] and LoRA-Edit [113] tune on each source video. Tune-A-Video adapts an image diffusion model from one textvideo pair with spatiotemporal attention and DDIM inversion, and LoRA-Edit applies mask-aware LoRA tuning to an image-to-video model, taking structure and motion from the source and edited appearance from reference images. Video2LoRA [523] avoids per-reference optimization: hypernetwork predicts reference-specific LoRA weights in one forward pass.

sections.title: 5.5 Applications
sections.content: Generated video serves as content, as an avatar, as visual plan, or as training data, and each use places different demands on conditioning, latency, consistency, and evaluation. Systems that also model actionconditioned transitions are treated in Section 7.

sections.title: 5.5.1 Creative Content Production
sections.content: Video generation enters production at several stages, from concept shots and storyboards to narrative footage, advertising and educational variants, and visual-effects edits. The agentic systems of Section 5.3.5 handle planning and tool orchestration, while foundation generators increasingly bundle creation and revision operations. Following Sora [31], Movie Gen [372] combines text-to-video generation with personalization, instruction-based editing, and synchronized audio. Closed systems such as Kling [224] and Sora 2 [360] offer textand image-to-video generation as products, and Sora 2 adds synchronized audio. Open models such as VideoCrafter2 [48], Open-Sora [648], Wan [462], HunyuanVideo [219], and Step-Video-T2V [328] make text-to-video generation available through released weights. Seedance 1.0 [120] adds native multi-shot generation with consistent subjects, and Seedance 2.0 [442] accepts text, image, audio, and video inputs for joint audio-video generation, reference-based generation, and editing. Production also needs what per-clip realism does not measure: keeping character, location, or style across shots, revising one element without disturbing the rest, and controlling camera and motion. These needs tie personalization and control (Section 5.4) to cross-shot and preference evaluation (Section 5.1.2).

sections.title: 5.5.2 Avatars and Character Animation
sections.content: Avatar generation maps speech, motion, or other control signals to the visible behavior of person or character. Its lineage runs through the audio-driven systems of Section 5.1: Wav2Lip [375] edits the mouth region with lip-sync expert, and SadTalker [626] predicts expression and head-pose coefficients of 3D face model. Diffusion models such as EMO [446] and Hallo [542] generate expressive portrait motion directly from audio, and VLOGGER [75] extends the output to the upper body with hand and gesture motion from single reference image. Pose-driven animation, as in Animate Anyone [179] and MagicAnimate [548], replaces audio with motion sequence and is judged against that motion instead of speech. In both settings, identity, clothing, background, and non-speech motion must stay stable over long or varied inputs. Real-time avatars must also produce frames at sustained rate with bounded delay while staying synchronized with incoming audio or motion. MuseTalk [633] dubs video in latent space and reports 30 frames per second at 256 256 resolution on V100 GPU. Vidu S1 [616] lets voice instructions redirect an ongoing character stream, and Vidu S2 [615] adds references that can be updated during streaming and frame-aligned editing of an incoming video stream. Mid-stream control adds action-to-output latency to throughput as criterion and links avatars to the real-time interactive world models of Section 7.2.3.

sections.title: 5.5.3 Video Plans for Embodied Agents
sections.content: Generated video can serve as plan between task specification and physical execution, and methods differ mainly in how they recover actions from it. UniPi [87] generates future video from text task and extracts controls with an inverse dynamics model, using images as planning space shared by embodiments with different action spaces. AVDC [215] infers actions from dense correspondences between generated frames, so 40 Video Foundation Models World-Modeling Lens policies can be learned from videos without action labels. RoboDreamer [656] composes video predictions of reusable instruction primitives to generalize to new objectaction combinations, and Dreamitate [269] fine-tunes video model on human demonstrations and tracks the generated tool motion to control robot. generated plan stays fixed, whereas an interactive simulator such as UniSim [561] updates its predictions as actions arrive (Section 7).

sections.title: 5.5.4 Synthetic Data for Embodied AI and Driving
sections.content: Embodied and driving systems need observations of rare tasks, environments, and failures that are costly or unsafe to collect. Video generation can supply them offline by varying appearance, layout, traffic, camera pose, or actions while keeping the annotations carried by the condition. In driving, MagicDrive [116] conditions multi-camera street views on camera poses, road maps, 3D bounding boxes, and text with cross-view attention, and Panacea [503] generates annotated multi-view videos from birds-eye-view layouts. DriveDreamer [476] and GAIA-1 [172] go further and predict future driving observations under scene or action conditions (Section 7). In robotics, the data must also carry actions: DreamGen [198] adapts an image-to-video model to target embodiment and labels its generated trajectories with latent-action or inverse-dynamics model. GigaWorld-0 [441] pairs controllable video generator with 3D generation and system identification to train vision-language-action policies (Section 7). Generated data are judged by downstream perception and policy results on real observations, not by visual fidelity. INSIGHT Rendering fidelity and stateful control are distinct scaling axes Video priors increasingly make each clip convincing, yet visual fidelity and stateful control are separate goals. good control changes only its target, keeps that change over time, and combines with other controls without disturbing identity, geometry, or motion. Progress should therefore be measured by comparing matched rollouts with and without the control, not by the quality of each rollout alone.

sections.title: 6 T Unified Video Models: Sharing the World
sections.content: Sharing means understanding and generation use common representations, parameters, interfaces, or objectives. Video understanding and generation have traditionally relied on separate encoders and generators. Unified video models implement the sharing relation of Section 2: inferred content can condition generation, and generative structure can support understanding and reasoning. Definition 2.6 evaluates sharing at three levels: capability coverage (one system performs both directions), architectural sharing (the directions use common components), and functional synergy (one direction improves the other under controlled comparison). We cover systems with video input or output that link understanding and generation, and cite image-only work where it supplies design or evaluation protocol missing for video.

sections.title: 6.1 Unified Architectures
sections.content: Unified architectures differ in where understanding and generation meet (Figure 8): in shared token sequence, shared continuous latent space, semantic bridge between decoupled experts, or the task state of an agent that calls specialized tools. Table 14 compares representative video systems along the component dimensions of Zhao et al. [640]. The first three families have image-domain precedents: Chameleon [439] for early-fusion token sequences, Transfusion [650] for autoregressive text and diffusion images in one Transformer, Janus [508] for decoupled encoders, and MetaQueries [363] for learned-query bridges. sections.title: 6.1.1 Discrete-Token Unification
sections.content: Discrete-token models convert text, images, and video into symbols that are interleaved in one sequence. single Transformer then serves both directions with next-token prediction: answering predicts text tokens after video context, and generation predicts visual tokens after text or visual condition. Emu3 [479] follows this design without diffusion heads, covering image and video understanding and generation, and Emu3.5 [76] scales the same objective to video-heavy data and reports world-modeling behavior such as spatiotemporally 43 (cid:71)(cid:35) (cid:71)(cid:35) (cid:71)(cid:35) (cid:71)(cid:35) (cid:71)(cid:35) (cid:71)(cid:35) (cid:71)(cid:35) Video Foundation Models World-Modeling Lens consistent exploration. Video-LaVIT [206] cuts the token cost of video by tokenizing keyframes and motion separately, and VILA-U [521] trains its vision tower to align discrete tokens with language while keeping the detail needed for generation. SEED-LLaMA [123] pairs discrete visual tokens with diffusion image decoder; it answers video questions but generates only images. Two variants change the role of the tokens or the objective: Vega [486] predicts semantic keyframe tokens autoregressively and leaves appearance to diffusion renderer, and NExT-OMNI [323] replaces autoregression with discrete flow matching over text, image, video, and audio tokens. This route gives many inputoutput combinations one vocabulary, one sequence format, and one likelihood objective. However, the tokenizer becomes the bottleneck: codes must preserve appearance and motion without making sequences unmanageably long, and quantization discards information before the Transformer sees it. Long autoregressive outputs also accumulate errors through their generated prefix.

sections.title: 6.1.2 Continuous Latent-Space Unification
sections.content: Continuous latent-space models avoid quantization: an encoder maps images or video into continuous feature space that an understanding head reads and decoder, diffusion model, or flow head turns back into pixels. The latent space is shared, but the losses and output heads can differ, because language prediction and pixel generation have different numerical requirements. TUNA [306] cascades VAE encoder with representation encoder, and Show-o2 [531] replaces the discrete vocabulary of Show-o [530] with 3D causal VAE; both predict text autoregressively and generate images and video with flow matching. Uni-ViGU [382] starts from the other end, extending video diffusion generator with discrete flow matching for text and lightweight understanding layers. AToken [311] and HYDRA-X [609] make the tokenizer itself the shared component, training it with reconstruction and semantic objectives over images, video, and, for AToken, 3D. PixelUMM [499] drops the pretrained encoder and VAE: pixel patches and video tubelets enter mixture-of-transformers in which the two directions keep separate projections and feed-forward layers but share attention, supporting video question answering, generation, and editing. Continuous spaces fit diffusion and flow generators naturally, but they expose tension that recurs across unified models. Understanding benefits from invariance to texture and small appearance changes, whereas generation must retain enough detail to reconstruct them.

sections.title: 6.1.3 Decoupled and Modular Unification
sections.content: Decoupled systems sidestep this tension by keeping separate visual pathways for the two directions, linked through an LLM, projection layer, or learned adapter. The understanding encoder can drop nuisance detail and emphasize objects, relations, actions, or text, while separate tokenizer or decoder keeps the fine spatial and temporal detail needed to generate video. NExT-GPT [516] and GPT4Video [489] set the modular baseline around an instruction-following LLM and frozen pretrained encoders and generators, so only small part of the system is trained: NExT-GPT links the LLM to diffusion decoders through lightweight projections, whereas GPT4Video has the LLM write textual prompts for an off-the-shelf text-to-video model. Later systems train the bridge. Omni-Video [435], UniVid [317], and UniVideo [498] let an MLLM interpret the instruction and pass continuous features through an adapter or bridge to diffusion decoder; UniVid adds reflection mechanism for temporal reasoning. Omni-Video 2 [557] keeps the MLLM frozen and conditions the decoder on predicted target caption and source-video latents for editing, and ReViSE [298] trains an Omni-Video model with feedback from its own VLM (Section 6.2.4). Other systems redesign the bridge itself. Lumos-Nexus [534] aligns small generator with the understanding model and mixes its velocity predictions with those of larger pretrained generator at inference. MoRoute [114] learns which layer of frozen VLM conditions each diffusion block, and Mamoda2.5 [413] feeds semantic features to sparse-expert diffusion backbone through learned queries. Lance [111] replaces the bridge with shared attention: separate semantic and VAE encoders feed dual experts that attend over one interleaved sequence. JavisGPT [287] extends the encoderLLMdecoder pattern to sounding video, passing synchrony-aware queries to joint audiovideo generator. Decoupling keeps strong pretrained components and makes each one replaceable. However, the bridge can become an information bottleneck: semantic clue sufficient for following an instruction may omit the 44 Video Foundation Models World-Modeling Lens Figure 9 Learning paradigms in unified video models. Isolated learning keeps independently pretrained experts; dual learning relates inverse tasks or reconstruction cycles; co-learning optimizes both directions jointly; and synergistic learning targets cross-direction benefit. The paradigms can coexist. appearance, geometry, or motion that the decoder needs.

sections.title: 6.1.4 Agentic and Tool-Augmented Unification
sections.content: Agentic systems leave perception, generation, editing, and evaluation to specialized models. controller reads the request and media, plans operations, calls tools, inspects their outputs, and revises the plan; what is shared is task state such as script, shot plan, prompt, edit graph, or critique. VideoAgent (editing) [653] plans shots and retrieves source clips before calling library of editing agents, and VISTA [307] wraps video generator in loop of temporal planning, candidate selection, multimodal critique, and prompt rewriting. UniVA [270] plans and calls understanding, generation, editing, and segmentation tools that share global, task, and user memories. Agents can combine strong tools without forcing their internal representations to agree, and each tool can be swapped as better models appear. However, they depend on tool selection, intermediate formats, and evaluator reliability: one wrong caption, retrieval result, or critique can redirect the whole workflow.

sections.title: 6.2 Learning Paradigms
sections.content: Architecture fixes where understanding and generation meet; training determines what signal flows between them (Figure 9). Isolated learning connects independently trained experts, dual learning relates the two directions through inverse or cycle objectives, co-learning optimizes both over shared parameters or representations, and synergistic learning uses one direction to improve the other. The paradigms can coexist; for example, cycle objective can be part of joint training.

sections.title: 6.2.1 Isolated Learning
sections.content: Isolated learning trains understanding and generation as independent experts and connects them after pretraining through small trained module, while most expert parameters stay frozen. NExT-GPT [516] 45 Video Foundation Models World-Modeling Lens and GPT4Video [489] follow this recipe (Section 6.1), as GILL [216] did for frozen language model and frozen image generator. Isolated learning is cheap and modular, and the source of each capability stays easy to identify. However, generation losses never update the video encoder and understanding losses never update the decoder, so no cross-direction transfer can occur, which makes isolated systems the natural baseline for measuring what tighter coupling adds.

sections.title: 6.2.2 Dual Learning
sections.content: Dual learning treats understanding and generation as approximately inverse problems: model reconstructs condition from generated content, regenerates an observation from an inferred representation, or enforces agreement over round trip. Such objectives let one direction supervise the other when paired labels are scarce. As many videos fit one description and one condition allows many valid futures, video cycle must preserve task-relevant events, identities, viewpoints, and motion while tolerating appearance variation. Uni-ViGU [382] is the clearest video-native example. Starting from video generator, it recovers understanding as the inverse task: it first reconstructs prompts to recall learned textvideo associations and then trains on detailed captions, keeping the original generation path. Dedicated cycle objectives remain image-based: CyCLeGen [405] couples imagelayout cycles, UniCorn [98] distills textimagetext self-play among proposer, solver, and judge roles, and Reconstruction Alignment [529] trains model to reconstruct an image from its own understanding embeddings.

sections.title: 6.2.3 Co-learning
sections.content: Co-learning optimizes understanding and generation objectives in one shared model or jointly trained bridge, and each of the first three families of Section 6.1 supports it. Discrete-token models such as Emu3 [479], Video-LaVIT [206], and VILA-U [521] apply one next-token objective to both directions, while Vega [486] shapes shared semantic token space and keeps separate diffusion renderer. Continuous and hybrid models share visual space or Transformer but keep distinct losses, as in TUNA [306], Show-o2 [531], HYDRA-X [609], PixelUMM [499], and the single-Transformer HaploOmni [527]. BAGEL [81] co-trains mixture of transformer experts that share attention but keep direction-specific projections and feed-forward layers, design Lance applies to video (Section 6.1). Bridge models such as Omni-Video [435], UniVid [317], and UniVideo [498] co-train the adapter between an MLLM and video decoder. Joint training creates an optimization imbalance between the two objectives. Understanding data rewards semantic invariance and concise answers, whereas generation data rewards retaining appearance and motion detail. Differences in dataset scale, loss magnitude, and convergence speed can let one direction dominate the shared parameters, so the data mixture and schedule decide how strongly each capability updates the model. Lance [111] counters this interference with staged multitask training and adaptive data scheduling. Tong et al. [452] study related choices when pretraining Transfusion-style backbone from scratch, comparing representation autoencoders, data mixtures, and dense or sparse-expert architectures with compute-matched imagetext analyses.

sections.title: 6.2.4 Synergistic Learning
sections.content: Synergistic learning uses one direction to improve the other; its evidence is measured gain in the receiving direction. From understanding to generation, OmniWeaving [362] conditions video generator on an MLLM that can first write reasoning trace about interleaved text, image, and video inputs; after end-to-end training, enabling this thinking mode raises its scores on intent-driven and interpolative tasks of IntelligentVBench. ReViSE [298] turns understanding into training signal for editing: the frozen VLM inside an OmniVideo model scores one-step estimate of the edited video, and its answer-token probabilities serve as differentiable reward alongside flow matching. Ablations against supervised fine-tuning on RVE-Bench support this understanding-to-editing transfer. Lances data-mixture ablations [111] give video evidence in both directions: adding understanding data improves generation on VBench, and adding generation data improves understanding on MVBench. From generation to understanding, Uni-ViGU [382] transfers generators textvideo associations through inverse-task training (Section 6.2.2), and Thinking with Video [451] generates intermediate frames at inference 46 Video Foundation Models World-Modeling Lens (Section 6.3.2). CounterVid [374] transfers through data: it synthesizes counterfactual action clips and trains video-language model with preference objective, reducing action and temporal hallucinations more than generic visual negatives do. UnityVideo [185] jointly learns depth, flow, segmentation, pose, and other visual conditions, improving both world-aware generation and the prediction of those signals. Gen4U [213] and GenCeption [468] reuse frozen or adapted video diffusion features for perception (Section 4.2). Integrated tasks provide third kind of evidence. UniUGP [310] tests whether scene reasoning and predicted video improve driving trajectories within one system (Section 6.3.3). EWAM [466] shows that masking or counterfactually replacing predicted-future features changes manipulation policys actions and success. Tong et al. [452] also find that general multimodal pretraining data, especially raw video, helps offline navigation planning through action-conditioned prediction. Apart from Lances data-mixture ablations, controlled bidirectional tests remain image-based (Section 6.4).

sections.title: 6.3 Applications
sections.content: Applications test whether information passed between understanding and generation improves task outcome.

sections.title: 6.3.1 Instruction-Driven Video Editing and Creation
sections.content: Instruction-driven editing follows readmodifywrite pattern: the model identifies the entities, events, motion, and time span an instruction refers to, then changes them while preserving everything else. plausible output is still wrong if it edits the wrong interval, loses subject identity, or damages surrounding content. Unified models place both steps in one system: Omni-Video [435] and UniVideo [498] pass MLLM interpretations to diffusion decoder (Section 6.1), and UNIC [576] casts editing as in-context generation over one shared sequence. ReViSE [298] adds reasoning to editing data: it pairs reasoning-enriched instructions with target edits and separates modifying clip from generating plausible continuation. Agentic systems extend editing into production workflows: VideoAgent (editing) [653] plans and assembles multi-shot edits, and VISTA [307] uses its own critiques to rewrite prompts across rounds (Section 6.1). Evaluation should therefore score localization, preservation of untouched content, and improvement across rounds, not only the quality of the final video.

sections.title: 6.3.2 Generative Reasoning
sections.content: Generative reasoning uses generation as an intermediate computation. video can show changing configuration that is hard to express in one image or textual chain of thought, as objects move, occlusions change, and the consequences of an operation unfold. The generated sequence then serves as an inspectable hypothesis about the process. Thinking with Video [451] uses video generator to produce intermediate frames during multimodal reasoning and evaluates them on VideoThinkBench. OpenCoF [58] trains chain-of-frame generation on temporally organized reasoning videos, while MME-CoF-Pro [321, 378] shows that answer accuracy can rise while intermediate frames stay inconsistent or hallucinated. ProAR [408] makes autoregressive video diffusion prospective by predicting its own goal frame alongside each chunk. However, generated reasoning traces add failure mode: coherent but unsupported intermediate video can make later answer look well grounded. Reliable use thus needs observed evidence separated from generated hypotheses, and tests of whether the intermediate video changes the answer for the right reason.

sections.title: 6.3.3 Unified Perception-Generation-Planning Systems
sections.content: In planning, generated video predicts what an action will do: the system reads the current observation, predicts how the scene may evolve under plan, and uses that prediction to choose or refine the action. Its value lies in the resulting decision, not in visual quality. UniUGP [310] applies this loop to autonomous driving: from multi-frame observations and instructions, its hybrid experts produce scene reasoning, future video, and trajectory, connected through four-stage curriculum. The question is whether future generation improves planning in difficult or long-tail situations. VideoAgent (planning) [423] applies the same idea to embodied tasks, refining generated video plans through self-conditioning and execution feedback. 47 Video Foundation Models World-Modeling Lens Table 15 Evidence ladder for unified video models, from separate competence to measured cross-direction transfer. sections.title: 6.4 Evaluation
sections.content: Table 15 expands the sharing row of Table 2 into evaluation levels: separate competence, integrated behavior, and measured synergy. Video coverage is mature at the first level, emerging at the second, and mostly directional at the third. Levels 1 and 2 refine the capability-coverage level of Definition 2.6 and Level 3 its functional-synergy level; architectural sharing is property of the design (Section 6.1), not benchmark score, and decision utility is covered by the integrated tasks of Section 6.2.4.

sections.title: 6.4.1 Per-Direction Evaluation
sections.content: Each direction is evaluated with its own communitys protocols: MVBench [248], Video-MME [109], LongVideoBench [509], LVBench [472], and MLVU [654] for understanding (Section 4.1), and VBench [193] and VBench-2.0 [647] for generation (Section 5.1.2). Results should be reported separately, since perceptual and faithfulness criteria are not interchangeable with question-answer accuracy. Matched single-task baselines can also reveal interference, where joint training improves one direction but degrades the other.

sections.title: 6.4.2 Unified, Interleaved, and Synergy Evaluation
sections.content: Integrated benchmarks test whether one system handles wider family of inputoutput transformations. UniVBench [501] is the most direct video-centered example: it evaluates understanding, generation, editing, and reconstruction on multi-shot videos with shared agentic evaluator, and its reconstruction and editing tasks check whether source content survives. RVE-Bench [298] and VR-Bench [534] test whether reasoningconditioned edits and generations do what the inferred intent implies, and UniVA-Bench [270] scores agentic workflows on both final media and planning behavior. UniM [257] extends input and output to text, image, video, and audio, while MME-Unify [533] covers integrated tasks in imagetext settings. Synergy evaluation instead compares matched routes, such as understanding-guided generation against plain generation, or understanding with and without generated intermediates. Image-domain studies lead here: DreamLLM [85] was an early study of synergy between understanding and generation in interleaved 48 Video Foundation Models World-Modeling Lens documents, and Uni-MMMU [668], RealUnify [412], and UniSandbox [353] score both directions with coupled tasks, matched routes, or decoupled tracks. UniG2U-Bench [504] finds that an extra generation step helps understanding on tasks that need visual transformation but can be neutral or harmful elsewhere. PseudoUnification [562] probes internal information patterns and finds divergent processing behind nominally shared parameters. Video evidence so far comes from training ablations and interventions and is mostly directional (Section 6.2.4); Section 8.3 discusses what video synergy test would need.

sections.title: 6.4.3 Protocols and Consistency
sections.content: Round-trip evaluation tests whether content survives an understandinggeneration cycle: model infers an event or layout, renders it, and reads it back, or generates video, describes it, and regenerates it. Existing round-trip training objectives are image-based (Section 6.2.2), and the reconstruction task of UniVBench is the closest video protocol. video protocol must name entities, event order, geometry, or dynamics to keep, score intended changes separately, and add non-unified and no-cycle controls. Reliable measurement also needs information controls. Traintest overlap can confound transfer with memorization, intermediate representations can leak answers across directions, and text accuracy, video fidelity, and cross-modal consistency may rely on different, possibly biased judges. UniSandbox [353] reduces leakage with synthetic tasks and separated modules, TorchUMM [324] standardizes model interfaces and task implementations, and UniSAFE [232] evaluates safety across inputoutput modality combinations. Judges can themselves be unified: UnifiedReward [485] trains one reward model to rank and score image and video outputs for both understanding and generation. INSIGHT Synergy requires controlled cross-direction transfer Shared tokens or parameters show coupling, separate scores show competence, and mixed inputoutput tasks show interoperability. Synergy needs controlled comparison: ablate the cross-direction path under matched data, capacity, and compute, and measure the change in generation, understanding, or an integrated task. 7 (cid:132) Video World Models: Interacting with the World Interacting means modeling state transition itself: how an established world evolves over time and, when actions, controls, or new observations are supplied, how they change that evolution. Interacting is the operation of Section 2: the model advances its state, st+1 pθ(st+1 st, at, ct), and decodes observations when visible output is needed. Rollout exposes failures that single plausible clip hides: generated errors feed back as context, off-screen content is forgotten, smooth motion breaks physical or causal structure, and actions miss their intended effects. We first place current models in the taxonomy of Section 3.4, then examine control, memory, responsiveness, grounding, applications, and evaluation. Zhu et al. [665] survey general world models starting from Sora; this chapter focuses on video-centered state.

sections.content: Crossing the two axes of Section 3.4 gives the 2 3 grid of Figure 10. cell describes how model is trained and used, so one model can occupy several cells: an action-conditioned latent predictor can score fixed candidate actions or run inside planner that acts, observes, and replans. Likewise, the attention pattern does not decide the column; model is interactive when it accepts new controls between emitted frames or chunks. Action-conditioned learning needs synchronized observations and controls, such as the DROID robot demonstrations [209] that train the action-conditioned V-JEPA predictors. Open X-Embodiment [357] pools robot data across embodiments in one format, although action units and coordinate frames still need alignment. sections.title: 7.1.1 Observation-Space Passive Prediction
sections.content: Passive visual models predict future observations from history alone. They can represent uncertainty over several plausible futures, as the action-free setting of SV2P [11] does by sampling latent variables to predict multiple future frames. Large video generators used as forecasters also belong here: Sora [31] was presented as step toward world simulation, Physics-IQ [346] scores how such generators continue real initial segment, and the base video-to-world models of Cosmos [355] predict futures from video prefix before any actionconditioned post-training. Training targets the next frame or future segment with reconstruction, likelihood, adversarial, diffusion, or flow losses. Autoregressive models feed their predictions back as history, whereas block predictors generate pending segment jointly. Passive prediction supplies dynamics priors and uncertainty estimates for the controlled cells.

sections.title: 7.1.2 Observation-Space Action-Conditioned Prediction
sections.content: This cell receives the controls for whole predicted segment before generation, such as ego motion, robot trajectory, camera poses, road layout, or planned object states. GAIA-1 [172] predicts discrete image tokens conditioned on text and action tokens before decoding video, and DrivingWorld [180] predicts driving observations together with ego state. Conditions range from ego dynamics, agent configurations, and road semantics (GAIA-2 [399]) and commands, goal points, and trajectories (Vista [118]) to frame-level robot actions (IRASim [663]). DriveDreamer [476] and post-trained Cosmos variants [355] condition on birds-eye-view maps, 3D boxes, and camera configurations. Most models in this cell adapt pretrained video generator through condition encoders, cross-attention, or control branches, and add structure, multi-view, or action-fidelity losses to the visual objective. Making them interactive requires causal generation that accepts new controls during rollout. Vid2World [189] makes video diffusion model autoregressive and action-guided, minWM [638] combines control tuning, autoregressive training, and few-step distillation, and BiWM [397] keeps bidirectional computation within causal generation. 50 Video Foundation Models World-Modeling Lens Table 16 Video world-model implementations and evaluated protocols. sections.title: 7.1.3 Observation-Space Interactive World Models
sections.content: Interactive visual models generate causally: emitted frames become history, and each new action changes the future that has not yet been generated. Genie [32] predicts video tokens from learned latent actions, GameNGen [459] diffuses the next game frame from past frames and actions, and DIAMOND [4] both trains policies inside its generated observations and runs as an interactive simulator. GameFactory [587] extends playable generation to newly constructed scenes, and Matrix-Game [631] couples visual context to keyboard and mouse input, with later version [156] adding chunked, few-step streaming diffusion. Oasis [79] renders playable Minecraft-like world from keyboard and mouse input in real time, Hunyuan-GameCraft [244] maps keyboard and mouse actions into shared camera representation and conditions on hybrid history to keep long play consistent, and Genie 3 [367] generates worlds from text prompts that users navigate in real time for several minutes. Controls can also be speech, and several actors can share one world. Vidu S1 and S2 [615, 616] take speech and updated references as controls on streaming character (Section 5.5), and Wan-Streamer [188] keeps audio-visual context to respond full-duplex to incoming events (Section 7.2.3). Solaris [402] pairs synchronized actions and observations from two Minecraft players, and MultiWorld [510] binds actions to agent identities and updates shared geometry-aware representation between chunks, so that every actor affects the same world.

sections.title: 7.1.4 Latent-State Passive Prediction
sections.content: Latent passive models predict video-derived features without actions, often as pretraining for later transition models. V-JEPA [20] learns by predicting the features of masked video regions, and the pretraining stage 51 Video Foundation Models World-Modeling Lens of V-JEPA 2 [9] scales this objective over images and video. Because the masked region can be predicted from frames on both sides, this objective is not causal forecasting; future prediction requires separate, causal protocol. We keep these models in the taxonomy because their predictors supply the feature space and initialization of the action-conditioned latent cells; on their own, they are pretraining for transition models rather than complete world models. Later variants change the prediction unit or the loss. Causal-JEPA [349] infers masked object-level latents from surrounding objects to encourage relational prediction. V-JEPA 2.1 [348] adds dense context-token loss and multi-level supervision for stronger local structure.

sections.title: 7.1.5 Latent-State Action-Conditioned Prediction
sections.content: Adding actions keeps feature-space target but conditions its evolution on controls. V-JEPA 2-AC [9] post-trains predictor on robot trajectories, DINO-WM [652] learns how frozen DINOv2 features evolve under actions, and LeWorldModel [334] instead learns the encoder and predictor jointly from pixels with latent regularization. V-JEPA 2.1 also trains diffusion predictor over its features for navigation [348]. Such models can roll candidate action sequence forward and compare the result with goal representation without rendering single frame. LaDi-WM [192] predicts geometric and semantic features for manipulation policy, and MoWM [593] combines motion-aware latent prediction with pixel-space signals. The JEPA-WM design study [444] compares encoders, proprioception, context, multi-step losses, and planning optimizers in one recipe and finds that the best combination depends on the task.

sections.title: 7.1.6 Latent-State Interactive World Models
sections.content: An interactive latent system closes the loop with model predictive control (MPC): the planner chooses an action prefix, executes it, encodes the new observation, and plans again. V-JEPA 2-AC [9] and DINO-WM [652] use this loop, and V-JEPA 2.1 [348] applies it to reaching, grasping, and pick-and-place on real robot arm. H-JEPA [625] stacks latent spaces at coarser timescales so that upper levels supply subgoals to lower-level planning. Latent rollout spends no capacity on texture and scores candidates without decoder, but latent distance can omit task-relevant details. Because corrective replanning can hide poor scores, scorer-level audits complement closed-loop success (Section 7.4). INSIGHT Rendering, causal rollout, and decision state can be specialized visual generator can supply appearance and motion priors, an online generator can provide action-conditioned rollout, and latent predictor can supply compact state for planning. These components need not share representation or training stage, but for the same history and action their rendered consequences, retained state, and decision scores must agree.

sections.title: 7.2 Core Technical Challenges
sections.content: Four challenges recur across the grid: control, memory, latency, and physical grounding. Memory and physical consistency matter in every cell; controlled prediction must also bind each control to its consequence, and interaction must do so within response budget. The challenges interact: longer memory raises inference cost, fewer denoising steps change rollout stability, and stronger action constraints can disturb the visual prior inherited from pretraining.

sections.title: 7.2.1 Action-Conditioned Controllability
sections.content: Action control poses two problems. Without action records, latent-action model must learn control variable from observed transitions; with supplied controls, conditioning must bind each signal to the right time, view, object, and consequence. Latent action learning. Latent-action models couple inverse and forward dynamics. An inverse model infers variable that explains the change between two nearby frames, and forward model predicts the later frame from the earlier one and that variable. discrete codebook or continuous bottleneck limits how much information the variable carries, which favors compact control code. LAPO [403], LAPA [574], and Moto [61] use discrete latent actions to pretrain policies from unlabeled video, and Genie [32] uses them 52 Video Foundation Models World-Modeling Lens to make platformer videos playable. LAPA then maps its codes to robot commands with small labeled set, while Moto treats them as language of motion tokens. Continuous latent actions offer more capacity. AdaWorld [119] conditions an autoregressive world model on them and adapts to new action spaces with little interaction, while IGOR [57] encodes initial-to-goal image changes in one space for humans and robots. However, latent action can lock onto the wrong source of change. LAOM [351] shows that visual distractors lead latent actions to encode background or camera motion, whereas little action supervision anchors them to the agent. Latent codes should therefore be tested for decoding into executable actions and for transfer under distractors, not only for reconstruction. Action Forcing [430] avoids an unconstrained code: it recovers signed egomotion axes from principal components of tracked pixel motion and uses them as controls that can be tested for reversal, scaling, and composition. Action conditioning mechanisms. Known actions remove the discovery problem but must still be aligned with the frames they affect. single sequence embedding is too coarse when each frame must respond to different command, so IRASim [663] injects actions frame by frame throughout its diffusion Transformer. Other systems express controls where their effects appear. EA-WM [568] projects joint or end-effector kinematics into the camera view as visual action fields, and Aero-World [388] feeds acceleration and angular velocity as tokens and checks inertial consistency with frozen latent physics probe. X-World [646] conditions multi-camera driving on ego actions plus optional controls over traffic agents, road elements, and appearance. Models that predict both states and actions must also stay responsive to actions; FLEX-WAM [210] rebalances the two losses and tracks an action-sensitivity proxy for this purpose.

sections.title: 7.2.2 Long-Horizon Consistency and Memory
sections.content: Long-horizon failure occurs at two scales. Locally, small prediction errors return as context and accumulate across frames or chunks; globally, finite context drops entities, layouts, and events that are no longer visible. The first calls for aligning training histories with deployment, the second for storing, compressing, or recurrently updating information beyond the active window. TECO [552] is an early example, compressing past frames into temporally consistent latent codes to keep long rollouts coherent. Training-inference alignment: the forcing family. Under teacher forcing, the model predicts from clean ground-truth history, whereas at deployment it conditions on its own outputs, so small error in geometry or identity becomes the next input. Diffusion Forcing [44] exposes the model to uncertain histories by giving sequence elements independent noise levels; GameNGen similarly perturbs its conditioning frames with noise, and LIVE [187] adds forwardreverse cycle consistency. MAGI-1 [443] denoises chunks block-causally. Autoregressive diffusion adds second mismatch, between many-step bidirectional teacher and few-step causal student. CausVid [582] makes pretrained video diffusion model causal and distills its sampler through distribution matching, Self-Forcing [190] trains the student on its own rollouts, and Causal Forcing [664] distills from an autoregressive teacher whose sampling path already follows causal inference. Later variants change the denoising window (Rolling Forcing [290]), the prediction horizon (Next Forcing [537]), or the distillation objective (One-Forcing [104], Delta Forcing [522]); Table 17 lists their mechanisms and intended effects. Retrieval-augmented and structured memory. Retrieval extends the context with stored observations that are recalled when the camera or agent returns to relevant region. WorldMem [528] stores frames with pose and time metadata and attends to them to reconstruct earlier scenes; Context-as-Memory [586] retrieves only scene-relevant past views, and WorldWeaver [305] builds its memory on predicted depth, which drifts less than RGB. Spatial Memory Intelligence [566] uses multimodal LLM to cluster, sparsify, filter, and retrieve stored views by action, while Keepsake [1] caps the archive by evicting views that others can replace. Such archives trade growing storage and retrieval cost for detailed evidence that can be revisited. Geometry makes recall more precise and reduces false matches between similar-looking places. VMem [251] indexes views by 3D surfels, RELIC [171] stores compressed history with relative actions and absolute camera poses in its keyvalue (KV) cache, and AnchorWeave [495] retrieves local memories around persistent anchors. Long-term spatial memory [518] keeps reconstructed static point map for layout, recent frames for motion, and retrieved past frames for appearance. Matrix-Game 3.5 [381] keeps geometrically projected latent patches for the static scene and reference tokens for moving subjects, so that past positions of an object are not mistaken for additional objects. 53 Video Foundation Models World-Modeling Lens Table 17 Training mechanisms for causal and streaming generation. DMD: distribution-matching distillation. WorldDirector [465] conditions causal chunks on externally planned object and camera trajectories plus retrieved object crops, so planned objects keep moving while unseen. LiveWorld [90] keeps static background and localized dynamic entities and uses virtual monitors to generate their progress outside the view before projecting it back into the scene; its LiveBench checks this off-screen progression. Context compression. Compression keeps bounded working context. FramePack [619] gives older frames smaller representation budgets than recent ones and adds drift prevention to sampling. Fixed-size state representations. Fixed-size memories keep constant-size state and pay compression cost at every update. Long-context state-space world models [371] pair block-wise state-space scan with dense local attention, and Echo-Infinity [26] recurrently updates memory queries as frames leave its local window. GIM-World [502] encodes selected past latents into geometry-supervised tokens, and Owl-1 [191] keeps learned state queries inside multimodal LLM alongside predicted textual dynamics. Honeycomb [411] recurrently writes six fixed-size spatial and spatiotemporal feature planes that cover larger ranges at coarser resolution. WorldTrace [520] keeps fixed-size KV memory of averaged scene summaries and selected landmark keys that later queries can reach beyond the recent window, and evaluates it with its LoopBench revisit test. Recurrent states can drift, test-time weight updates [77] add optimization latency, and compact memories may drop details needed later for rendering. Retrieval, compression, and fixed state thus trade capacity against latency differently and can be combined  (Table 18)  .

sections.title: 7.2.3 Real-Time Responsiveness
sections.content: Responsiveness is the delay between new action and the first output that reflects it; slow transition breaks the control loop even when offline throughput is high. End-to-end cost combines sampling depth, work per step, active history, cache construction, latent decoding, and the rate at which controls enter the rollout. Recent systems report real-time rates: Vidu S1 [616] reaches up to 42 frames per second (FPS) at 540p on consumer GPUs, and Wan-Streamer [188] reaches 25 FPS. Display rate can still overstate responsiveness: with temporal compression, several frames are decoded per predicted latent, so actions may enter less often than frames 54 Video Foundation Models World-Modeling Lens Table 18 Memory mechanisms for long-horizon video generation and world modeling. Horizon scaling distinguishes active context from the full archive.
