Waypoint-1.5 [389], causal diffusion Transformer with bounded KV caches for keyboard-mouse play on consumer hardware, accordingly reports rendered and latent FPS and control rate separately. Few-step distillation and adversarial post-training. Training-based acceleration turns many-step generator into causal student with fewer evaluations per frame or chunk, as CausVid, Self-Forcing, and Causal Forcing do while aligning rollouts. Adversarial post-training goes further: Seaweed-APT [276] distills video diffusion model into one-step generator, AAPT [277] applies autoregressive adversarial post-training to real-time interactive video, and Causal Forcing++ [639] scales few-step autoregressive distillation. Once sampling depth is reduced, the backbone, active context, and decoder dominate the cost, and the student must also stay stable over long rollouts. Training-free acceleration. Training-free methods exploit redundancy at inference. Sparse attention suits streaming because the current query is short and the history long: Light Forcing [325] keeps the anchors and recent frames that control the next output. Caching reuses features that change little across denoising steps, as in TeaCache [281] and FasterCache [326]. WorldCache [107] adapts caching to world models, where an error in few control-sensitive action, image, or memory tokens can propagate through the rollout. TurboDiffusion [617] combines both routes, stacking step distillation with low-bit and sparse attention and weightactivation quantization, reporting two orders of magnitude of end-to-end acceleration on single consumer GPU.

sections.title: 7.2.4 Physical and Causal Grounding
sections.content: Physical grounding asks whether motion and interaction respect contact, rigidity, gravity, and persistence. Causal grounding asks how the predicted future changes when an action or initial condition is intervened on, and whether unaffected factors stay fixed. Current methods offer much machinery for plausible dynamics, whereas intervention-level supervision and evaluation remain less developed. 55 Video Foundation Models World-Modeling Lens Explicit physics simulation integration. Explicit methods let simulator produce the dynamics and generator render them. PhysGen [294] and PhysMotion [434] estimate object shape and material from single image, simulate the motion, and use it to guide video generation. PhysGen3D [43] extends this to interactive 3D scenes with user-set initial conditions, and PhysCtrl [463] instead replaces the simulator with generative physics network trained on simulated animations, conditioned on material parameters and forces. Mass, material, force, or initial velocity thus become editable, but deformable bodies, fluids, fracture, articulated agents, and partly observed contact remain hard to recover from pixels and to simulate. Implicit physics alignment. Implicit approaches keep learned generator and change what it learns from. VideoREPA [627] distills token-level relations from self-supervised video encoder, which carries stronger physical structure, into text-to-video generator. Phantom [409] couples visual trajectories with auxiliary physical latents, and RoboScape [407] trains with depth and temporal structure as additional targets. PhyGDPO [37] post-trains on preferences between candidate videos ranked by physical plausibility, and WROP [612] supplies procedurally generated Blender data for object permanence and solidity. Inference-time planning instead adds no physics training: VLIPP [564] uses vision-language model to plan coarse physical motion and converts the plan into structured noise for motion-controllable image-to-video diffusion model. Intervention-level causal evidence. Plausibility objectives do not record which force, action, or initial condition produced motion. Causal evidence instead holds the initial state fixed, varies one action or physical parameter, and compares both the affected future and the unchanged state. PhysEditWorld [173] supplies such data by replaying identical game episodes under different gravity settings, with synchronized video, action, engine-state, and parameter signals (see also Section 8.2). OneWorld [155] requires several action-conditioned futures of one scene to share latent physical explanation, scored by mechanism interpreter during flow training and sampling. Different actions should then change outcomes, not the worlds mechanism.

sections.title: 7.3 Applications
sections.content: Applications differ in who consumes the prediction. world model may produce dataset, train policy, evaluate policy, supply forecasts to planner, or respond directly to person. The first three support decisions before deployment, whereas planning and human simulation consume predictions online. The same action-conditioned generator can move between these roles as its control fidelity and temporal stability improve.

sections.title: 7.3.1 Data Engines
sections.content: As data engine, world model turns controllable variation into training examples where real observations are expensive, dangerous, or unevenly distributed. Each example must include the labels the learner needs, often actions. In robotics, DreamGen [198] and GigaWorld-0 [441] synthesize action-labeled trajectories for policy training (Section 5.5). In driving, the action-conditioned generators of Section 7.1.2, such as GAIA-2 [399], Vista [118], and Cosmos [355], supply unusual layouts and safety-critical cases that fleet logs rarely contain.

sections.title: 7.3.2 Policy Training in Imagination
sections.content: Imagination training keeps the world model inside the optimization loop: policy acts, the model predicts the next observation or state, and reward updates the policy. Unlike data engine, the generated distribution then follows the current policy, and errors compound along the trajectories it chooses. Action-conditioned video models such as UniSim [561], iVideoGPT [513], and Pandora [525] can serve as this simulator if their action effects, rewards, and resets are accurate enough. World-VLA-Loop [297] refines vision-language-action policies by reinforcement learning in world model that predicts future frames and binary rewards. It feeds the updated policys rollouts back into the model, since fixed simulator fails most often on states that changed policy visits. Dreamer 4 [147] trains Minecraft agent with reinforcement learning inside video world model learned largely from offline video and action data. Because each step of diffusion world model may need many denoising evaluations, Horizon Imagination [74] denoises several future observations in parallel and decouples the denoising budget from the rollout horizon, making longer on-policy rollouts affordable. 56 Video Foundation Models World-Modeling Lens

sections.title: 7.3.3 Policy Evaluation Environments
sections.content: For policy evaluation, world model replaces repeated deployment with reproducible generated trials. WorldGym [386] rolls out robot policies in an action-conditioned video model and scores them with visionlanguage model, while WorldEval [259] encodes policy behavior with Policy2Vec to drive its simulation. Both are validated by whether generated success rates preserve real-world policy rankings. Such agreement depends on the policies tested, since simulator tuned on familiar checkpoints may misrank controller that visits new states or exploits modeling artifact. Later systems add multi-view, memory-supported rollouts (Ctrl-World [140]) or task-progress and success judges (GE-Sim 2.0 [385]), and generalist robot (DreamDojo [117]) and driving (GAIA-3 [496]) world models list policy evaluation among their uses. OmniDreams [22] takes hybrid route in driving, generating sensor observations online inside the AlpaSim simulator, whose own services handle traffic and physics.

sections.title: 7.3.4 Predict-then-Act Planning
sections.content: Predict-then-act methods use forecast as evidence for the next decision and differ in how much of the future they decode. At the pixel end, UniPi [87] and AVDC [215] generate video plan and recover actions with an inverse-dynamics model or dense correspondences (Section 5.5). Such plans are easy to inspect but add generation cost and another source of error. Navigation World Models [18] instead predict egocentric observations under candidate navigation actions with conditional diffusion Transformer and plan by checking which simulated trajectory reaches the goal. VPP [181] instead conditions an inverse-dynamics policy on future-aware features from fine-tuned video diffusion model. LaDi-WM [192] and MoWM [593] combine latent prediction with feature or pixel signals, and LaWAM [51] predicts latent visual subgoals without reconstructing video. At the latent end, V-JEPA 2-AC and DINO-WM score candidate actions without decoding pixels, which cuts prediction cost but makes their forecasts harder to inspect. Prediction can also serve only as training supervision. WLA-0 [565] trains shared representations with future-frame World Expert and an Action Expert, so the World Expert can be dropped at test time or re-enabled to select among sampled action chunks.

sections.title: 7.3.5 Interactive Simulation for Humans
sections.content: In human-interactive simulation, world prediction is the application: person supplies actions, and the model produces the evolving observation stream. Among playable systems, Genie made unlabeled video playable and Genie 3 [367] opens text-prompted worlds to real-time exploration, GameNGen simulates an existing game in real time, and Oasis [79] and Matrix-Game 2.0 [156] target real-time open deployment. Yume [337] and RELIC [171] extend exploration to real-world scenes, with RELIC adding long-horizon memory for revisits. Voice-controlled streaming characters such as Vidu S1 and Wan-Streamer (Section 7.2.3) extend the input from game actions to speech, so response timing and turn-level coherence matter alongside visual continuity. In driving, GAIA-2, Vista, and Cosmos-Drive-Dreams [393] let users set trajectories, actions, or scene conditions and inspect the resulting futures. With fixed-control model, the user edits conditions between rollouts, whereas an interactive system accepts input within the stream.

sections.title: 7.4 Benchmarks and Evaluation
sections.content: World-model evaluation follows the role of the prediction. rendered future needs visual and motion quality, and an interactive simulator adds action fidelity, persistent state, and bounded response time. Planning, policy training, and policy evaluation further require the prediction to improve or faithfully estimate downstream decision. These requirements form the Interacting row of the evidence ladder in Table 2, from visual plausibility through controllable rollout to decision utility [592]. Table 19 indexes current benchmarks by the claim they test and the main limits on comparing their scores.

sections.title: 7.4.1 Challenge-Aligned Benchmarks
sections.content: Action following and controllability. Action benchmarks test whether changing control changes the predicted future as intended. ACT-Bench [7] measures instructionexecution consistency and trajectory error for driving 57 interfaces differ Static revisits alone do not test off-screen dynamics Display, latent, and control rates differ Intervention modalities differ Visual similarity alone does not establish state correctness Video Foundation Models World-Modeling Lens Table 19 World-model benchmarks and protocols by target, with limits on interpreting and comparing scores. Evaluation target Benchmarks / protocols Video plausibility VBench [193], VBench++ [194], VBench-2.0 [647] Interpretation limit No closed-loop action or hidden-state test Action response ACT-Bench [7], iWorld-Bench [96], MiraBench [563] Action spaces and control State persistence MIND [575], MemoBench [49], LoopBench [520] Interactive latency Waypoint-1.5 [389] and system protocols Physical validity Scene / semantic consistency Decision utility WorldModelBench [241], Physics-IQ [346], WorldBench [458], CRONOS [24], What-If World [34] EWMBench [600] WorldGym [386], WorldEval [259], WMBench [128], RoboWM-Bench [201], WorldArena [406], ARC-Bench [634] Action/policy ranking and executed task success are distinct outcomes Multiple dimensions WorldScore [89], WorldSimBench [383], WorldMark [546], WBench [583], WorldOlympiad [645], WorldRoamBench [545] Aggregate scores can hide dimension-specific failures Calibration C3 evaluation [339], PAWBench [376], CaliBench [400] Calibration targets and statistical tests differ maneuvers, and iWorld-Bench [96] separates trajectory following from visual quality and memory through unified action layer. In robotics, MiraBench [563] tests action following, physical adherence, and optimism under actions that should fail, which matters because simulator that turns failed actions into plausible successes misleads both policy training and evaluation. Since game key, camera pose, robot action chunk, and an ego trajectory need different error measures, reports should state the native action space, horizon, intervention frequency, and source of trajectory estimates. Long-horizon consistency and memory. Consistency asks how identity, geometry, and appearance degrade with duration even when content stays visible. Measuring this degradation requires scores stratified by video length. Memory tests instead remove content from view and check it later. Revisit benchmarks such as LoopBench [520] test static recall, comparing returns with the models own first visit. However, static cache passes revisit tests even when the world should have changed. MBench [624] separates entity, environment, and causal memory under occlusion and off-screen evolution, STEVO-Bench [331] hides an ongoing process and checks whether it advanced, and MemoBench [49] requires an object that changed out of view to return in its updated state. MIND [575] and WorldRoamBench [545] test memory during closed-loop or open-world interaction, the latter scoring memory separately from action following, visual drift, and controllability-gated physics. Memory Maze [368] poses the same retention question for navigation agents. These protocols score decoded video; latent-state models lack matching probes of drift and goal reachability. Real-time response. Latency is reported per system, usually as FPS or time to first response, and mixes model forward time with denoising steps, decoding, cache construction, input rate, and hardware. matched protocol would measure the delay from an actions arrival to the first affected frame, sustained throughput, and latency variance over long sessions, at stated resolution, precision, hardware, and action frequency. Physical, temporal, and causal validity. Physical evaluation ranges from prompt-based plausibility to comparison with recorded outcomes. Prompt-based suites such as VideoPhy and VideoPhy-2 [16, 17] are described in Section 5.1.2. PhyGenBench [341] organizes prompts by physical principle, and WorldModelBench [241] combines instruction following with checks for violations such as broken conservation. Physics-IQ [346] instead 58 Video Foundation Models World-Modeling Lens compares continuations of real initial segment with recorded outcomes, and PhyWorldBench [137] adds anti-physics prompts that test whether model can follow instructions that deliberately violate physics while staying logically consistent. Other suites probe specific factors. WorldBench [458] separates intuitive principles from quantities such as friction and viscosity, and CRONOS [24] varies viewpoint, scene, appearance, and category within controlled events. What-If World [34] pairs prompts that change one physical detail and scores both the outcome difference and the preservation of the environment. ChronoMagic-Bench [598] tests temporal direction through metamorphic and time-lapse processes such as growth or construction. Prompt-level and rendered contrasts cover only part of the intervention protocol of Section 7.2.4, which ultimately needs logged actions and real outcomes. Calibration of predicted futures. Stochastic world models should also produce the right spread of futures. PAWBench [376] and CaliBench [400] sample repeated futures from fixed input and compare the outcome distribution with reference probabilities or sets of valid outcomes, reporting separately how often outcomes can be scored. C3 [339] calibrates confidence rather than outcome frequencies: it trains probe that predicts whether latent prediction is accurate and evaluates it against accuracy labels.

sections.title: 7.4.2 Application-Aligned Benchmarks
sections.content: Application-aligned benchmarks measure predictions effect after another component consumes it, through policy-ranking agreement, optimization gains, planning success, executable action success, or data efficiency. For policy evaluation, WorldGym [386] and WorldEval [259] compare model-based success rates or rankings with real robot trials. WMBench, introduced with GigaWorld-1 [128], studies evaluator design with an ordinal score that separates correct from incorrect task outcomes and high from low visual fidelity. For planning, WorldPrediction [45] tests high-level state transitions and procedural ordering, using counterfactual distractors that remove low-level continuity shortcuts. World-in-World [614] places heterogeneous models behind shared action interface and measures closed-loop task success. Embodied benchmarks make predictions executable or check them against task requirements. RoboWMBench [201] converts generated manipulation videos into actions and executes them in physics simulator, so visually plausible but unexecutable motion earns little credit. EWMBench [600] separates scene consistency, motion correctness, and semantic alignment, showing that visually stable output can miss the task motion. WorldLens [267] and DrivingGen [658] evaluate driving models, from generation and reconstruction to action following, trajectory plausibility, and downstream tasks. WorldArena [406] places perceptual quality alongside data-engine, policy-evaluation, and planning utility and finds that the two rankings need not agree. Latent-state models need their own audits. ARC-Bench [634] tests whether frozen latent-distance objectives rank candidate actions by their executed outcome costs, reporting rank agreement and regret while varying the replanning frequency, since frequent replanning can mask poor scoring. PokeWorld [433] pushes visually identical objects with different mass, drag, and stiffness to ask whether these parameters can be decoded from the latent state and whether predicted action effects depend on them correctly.

sections.title: 7.4.3 Foundational and Comprehensive Benchmarks
sections.content: Foundational video benchmarks set the visual and temporal quality floor on which control, memory, and utility tests build. They include the generation suites VBench and VBench-2.0 [193, 647] (Section 5.1.2) and VBench++ [194], which adds image-conditioned generation and trustworthiness. Comprehensive world-model suites differ mainly in protocol. WorldScore [89] asks models to generate successive scenes along given camera trajectories and scores controllability, quality, and dynamics. WorldSimBench [383] pairs human-aligned perceptual assessment with manipulation test that turns generated video into control signals. WorldMark [546] and WBench [583] evaluate interactive generation through standardized action sequences and multi-turn episodes, respectively. WorldOlympiad [645] scores physical faithfulness, geometric consistency, and interaction fidelity across games, robotics, and open-domain video. Shared tooling helps hold data and controllers fixed across comparisons: the stable-worldmodel platform [333] provides common data interfaces, baselines, planners, and environments with controllable visual, geometric, and physical factors. 59 Video Foundation Models World-Modeling Lens INSIGHT From predictive state to intervention and utility Evidence for world model should match its transition protocol  (Table 2)  . Passive models show predictive structure, and controlled models must also change the world where an action acts and keep what it leaves untouched. Interactive systems must preserve those consequences under feedback, and decision applications must turn them into better choices.

sections.title: 8 Open Challenges and Future Directions
sections.content: Seven open problems span reading, writing, sharing, and interacting; each needs new methods and better tests. Current models share recurring limits: encoders rarely maintain predictive state, generators lose identity and physical constraints over time, unified models have yet to show controlled synergy, and interactive systems degrade as generated history accumulates. These limits, together with gaps in evaluation, action supervision, generalization, and uncertainty, define seven challenges: long-horizon consistency, physical and causal grounding, measurable synergy, standardized evaluation, control from unlabeled video, generalization across scenes and embodiments, and stochastic worlds with rare events.

sections.title: 8.1 Long-Horizon World Consistency
sections.content: Long-horizon consistency requires model to retrieve distant evidence, preserve state that is no longer visible, and render that state consistently in later predictions. Long-video understanding benchmarks [151, 472, 509, 654] mainly test the first of these (Section 4.1). Autoregressive generation and interaction add further difficulty: generated errors enter the history that later predictions depend on. Current methods balance recent and distant context [313, 619], store retrievable observations [171, 528], or compress history into recurrent or fixed-size memory [26, 502] (Section 7.2.2). However, most of them store what was visible, whereas predictive state must also track what changed off-screen; only few systems model such change explicitly [90, 465]. For example, hidden ice cube keeps its identity as it melts (Figure 11). Replaying the stored observation returns stale cube [49]. One method direction is memory that updates hidden state during occlusion, trained to predict how unseen entities evolve, instead of replaying stored frames. Such memory complements rollout training: LIVE [187] targets error growth through forwardreverse cycle consistency without any external memory, so the two address different failures and can be combined. Memory must also fit an interactive budget: uncapped archives grow with the rollout, and retention budgets [1] turn this growth into eviction decisions, so learning what to keep is itself research problem. Memory benchmarks [49, 545, 575, 624] now test revisits, occlusion, and off-screen change (Section 7.4). The next step is to vary rollout length and revisit distance separately and report degradation curves instead of one terminal score, so that rendering drift and state loss can be told apart. Latent-state models have no frames to score, so they need probes of Figure 11 Hidden state evolves during occlusion; replaying an old observation can miss that change. 60 Video Foundation Models World-Modeling Lens goal reachability, feature stability, and decision quality as the horizon grows. Consistency results should also report memory size, end-to-end latency, and action-update rate.

sections.title: 8.2 Physical and Causal Grounding
sections.content: Physical grounding can be tested at three increasingly demanding levels. Reading benchmarks [23, 395, 578] test whether model recognizes persistence, stability, contact, and counterfactual outcomes in observed events. Generation benchmarks [16, 17, 137, 241, 341, 598] ask whether synthesized outcome follows physical commonsense, named law, or the direction of an irreversible process (Section 5.1.2). Actionand parameter-conditioned models face stronger test: changing an action or physical parameter should change the affected outcome and leave unrelated state intact. For example, ball released with the same velocity under two gravity settings should follow different trajectories while the camera and background stay fixed (Figure 12). realistic continuation can still respond wrongly to gravity or alter unrelated state, so realism is not enough [173, 241]. Figure 12 Changing gravity alters the trajectory while unrelated scene properties remain fixed. Current methods add physics at different stages (Section 7.2.4): they align generator features with video encoder [627], simulate dynamics before rendering [294], condition generation on planned motion [564], reward geometric consistency [473], or retrieve videos of similar phenomena [69]. Each depends on an outside source: the teachers coverage, the recovered state and material parameters, the generators ability to follow the plan, or the quality of the feedback and retrieved evidence. Paired rollouts that change one physical parameter [173], production data with recorded branches [36], and coupled action-conditioned futures [155] provide the missing contrast between change and its effect. One direction combines these physics priors with intervention-paired data, with objectives that reward the intended change and penalize drift elsewhere. Evaluation should also diagnose failures: an arrow-of-time error, contact violation, and wrong response to an action all make clip implausible, but they implicate different model components and training signals. Recent intervention benchmarks [24, 34, 458] point toward common protocol: hold the initial state fixed, change one action or physical parameter, and test the changed outcome, the invariance of unrelated state, the first violated constraint, and when it appears. Applying the same interventions to reading questions, generated continuations, and closed-loop rollouts would make transfer across operations measurable.

sections.title: 8.3 Measurable Synergy in Unified Video Models
sections.content: Unified video models span discrete-token, continuous, and modular designs [306, 479, 486, 498, 609], and some route information from generation to understanding, from reasoning to generation, or into planning [310, 362, 382] (Sections 6.1 and 6.2.4). The open question is causal: how much of the gain comes from shared representations or information flow, and how much from additional data, parameters, or supervision? Video evidence of transfer is so far partial or one-directional: video-diffusion features support recognition and geometry [213, 468], an MLLMs reasoning trace raises generation scores [362], mixing data helps both tasks [111], frozen vision-language critic improves editing [298], and predicted features affect actions [466] (Section 6.2). Breadth suites [257, 501] catch regressions but not transfer, and image-domain synergy tests [412, 562] miss what video adds: transferred information must preserve temporal order, motion, identity, and evolving state. 61 Video Foundation Models World-Modeling Lens On the method side, each transfer path can be built as separate component that can be switched off, such as temporalanalysis loss on the generator or generated intermediate states passed to temporal reasoner. Round-trip consistency between inferred trajectories and rendered video can then serve as training signal as well as test. The test itself compares two systems with the same tasks, data, capacity, and compute that differ only in whether the crossdirection path is enabled (Figure 13). Temporal analysis should then improve event order, motion, identity, or physical dynamics in generation, and generated intermediate states should improve temporal inference or planning under the same observation and parameter budget. Round trips render an inferred trajectory or event graph and read it back, or analyze, revise, and regenerate rollout. Each task must define its invariants, because one description can match several valid videos, and the intermediate representation must not carry the answer verbatim [353]. Figure 13 Two systems with matched resources differ only in whether information passes between understanding and generation.

sections.title: 8.4 Standardized Evaluation of World Properties
sections.content: World-model evaluation now covers control, memory, physical validity, and decision utility as well as visual realism, but the resulting numbers are rarely comparable. Suites for generated video, action response, and broader world properties [7, 89, 96, 193, 267, 545, 546, 583, 645, 647] differ in prompts, control spaces, horizons, and judges (Section 7.4), so scores do not transfer across suites. For example, two predictors guiding the same robot may return video and features, respectively (Figure 14). Video allows visual and trajectory checks while features need state probes, and both need decision test, because either can score well on its native metric yet fail at control [592, 634]. Figure 14 Video and feature predictions need different probes, but both face the same decision test. reporting standard should first match the protocol to the models prediction space and transition interface (Section 3.4). Interactive models need mid-rollout interventions and latency tests, action-conditioned models need faithful responses to fixed controls, and passive predictors need held-out transition tests. Each result should state the horizon, action frequency, conditioning, and judge model, and claims should rise from visual to controllable-rollout to decision-utility evidence [592]  (Table 2)  . Real-time claims need control-to-display latency, sustained throughput, and latency variance, reported with hardware, resolution, denoising steps, and active context, because frames per second alone is ambiguous. Shared infrastructure [333] standardizes data readers, planning solvers, and environment variations. Fixedcandidate action ranking should accompany closed-loop success, because frequent replanning can hide poor scorer [634]. Integrity needs held-out environments and leakage-controlled synthetic tasks, because web-scale and synthetic training data make overlap hard to detect. On the method side, two tools need development in their own right: learned judges, which can inherit their source models blind spots and need validation against human ratings, and standard probes that read latent predictions without pixel decoder. 62 Video Foundation Models World-Modeling Lens

sections.title: 8.5 Scaling Control from Unlabeled Video
sections.content: Internet video covers objects, agents, and dynamics but usually lacks the action behind each transition. Latent-action methods [32, 61, 403, 574] infer actions as learned variable (Section 7.2.1), enabling the use of far more video than labeled datasets, but scale alone does not specify what the variable represents. For example, gripper may push block while the camera pans and windmill turns (Figure 15). Only the push is the agents action, yet latent code trained for reconstruction can absorb the camera and background motion while reproducing the clip. Distractor experiments confirm this and show that limited action supervision can substantially improve the recovered factors [351]. Figure 15 Action effects mix with camera and background motion. Reconstruction accuracy and codebook usage are thus weak evidence of control: useful latent action should predict controllable effects, stay stable under camera and background changes, and transfer through simple mapping. Several weak signals can push latent actions toward these properties. small labeled set can anchor latent dimensions to real controls, multi-view invariance can separate camera motion from scene change, temporal bottlenecks can discard details irrelevant to control, and paired interventions can mark which changes belong to the agent. Continuous latent actions [119], humanrobot shared representations [57], and egomotion controls from tracked pixel motion [430] move in this direction, while state-annotated data [36, 264] give stronger but narrower supervision. Pseudo-action generation offers another source of training pairs: video model produces trajectory and an inverse or latent-action model labels its controls. Such data helps only when the inferred action has the intended effect in controlled environment or real system; otherwise the generator and the labeller reinforce each others shortcuts. Evaluation should keep labeled subset with interventions and measure transfer under unseen cameras, backgrounds, scenes, and embodiments.

sections.title:
8.6 Generalization across Scenes and Embodiments
Scene generalization changes appearance, layout, ob-
jects, or local dynamics for the same body, as when a
robot enters a new room. Embodiment generalization
changes the body, sensors, action frequency, degrees
of freedom, or physical meaning of an action, as when
skills move from human hands to a robot arm.
sections.content: Zero-shot claims therefore depend on which factor is held out. V-JEPA 2-AC [9] transfers to new scenes without target data, but on robot type seen in post-training, not an unseen embodiment. Other methods adapt latent actions with limited interaction [119], generate target-domain experience [198, 441], or broaden the pretraining prior [587]. For example, training may cover human hand in lab and kitchen but robot only in the lab (Figure 16). Deploying the robot in the kitchen tests an unseen 63 Figure 16 held-out scenebody pair tests whether familiar factors compose while preserving action effects. Video Foundation Models World-Modeling Lens scenebody pair, where the representation and control mapping must still move the block to the target. Cross-embodiment transfer adds an alignment problem: the same semantic action may need different joints and timing on different bodies, while similar-looking motion can have different contact consequences. Current methods connect human and robot behavior through shared image-goal units [57] or map latent actions to robot commands with small labeled set [574]. method direction is to train such mappings to preserve effects, with objectives defined on outcomes such as object displacement, contact, and task completion instead of raw control values or token similarity. Evaluation should cross scenes, embodiments, sensors, and action spaces and test effect equivalence, controllability, and safety after transfer. Reports should state whether results are zero-shot, calibrated, or fully fine-tuned, and how much target data they used.

sections.title: 8.7 Stochastic Worlds and Rare Events
sections.content: One history can admit several valid futures, because other agents may act differently and relevant physical state may be hidden. deterministic predictor cannot express these alternatives, and squared-error training can favor an average of incompatible outcomes. Latent-variable predictors [11, 230] sample multiple futures, and controllable generators and data engines [118, 198, 355, 399, 441] can synthesize rare scenarios for training (Section 7). However, synthesis does not say how likely each outcome is: prompted collision supplies training case, whereas calibrated collision risk supports decision under uncertainty. For example, given fixed driving history and ego actions, pedestrian may wait, cross after the car passes, or step into its path (Figure 17). generator can render the rare crossing without assigning it reliable probability. One direction is to develop generators that assign calibrated outcome probabilities rather than merely produce diverse samples, using empirical event rates or justified simulator priors. Generated rare cases must be checked for physical feasibility, causal relevance, and downstream utility before entering training data, since prompting fixes which failures appear but not their frequencies. For fixed history and action sequence, distributional evaluation assesses whether samples cover distinct valid outcomes, exclude invalid ones, and match observed or simulated outcome frequencies. Diversity alone rewards arbitrary variation, and best-of-many scoring hides misplaced probability mass. Reports should therefore use proper scoring rules, calibration curves, and mode coverage at fixed sample budget, distinguish unreadable from invalid samples, and use sample sizes appropriate to event rarity. Repeatedsampling benchmarks [376, 400] and confidence calibration [339] are start (Section 7.4), but extending outcome-frequency tests from endpoints in limited scenarios to long, action-conditioned trajectories is open. Figure 17 Valid futures differ in frequency, and invalid and unreadable samples must be counted separately. INSIGHT Scaling world models needs interventions, not just more clips Passive video expands coverage but leaves hidden state, physical causes, cross-direction transfer, action semantics, and outcome probabilities underdetermined. Most of these challenges need data and protocols with interventions (known hidden changes, paired physical edits, matched ablations, labeled actions, held-out scenebody pairs, and observed event rates). Observational scale shows what co-occurs; interventions show what changes what. 64 Video Foundation Models World-Modeling Lens

sections.title: 9 Conclusion
sections.content: This survey has treated video as an observed trace of latent temporal world and used reading, (cid:210) writing, sharing, and (cid:132) interacting to organize how foundation models connect observations to represented state. Comprehension recovers what trace reveals; generation constructs traces from conditions; unification shares information and machinery between the two; and world modeling asks how represented state changes under conditions or actions. Within this framing, video world model is defined by the transition it learns, which predicts future video or video-derived features and runs passively, under fixed action sequence, or interactively (Section 3.4). The distinction between temporal coherence and world consistency (Definition 2.4) separates the quality of rendered video from evidence that model tracks the world state behind it. The next phase demands stronger evidence  (Table 2)  . Beyond perceptual fidelity and local coherence, claims about the world require state that survives occlusion, revisits, and long horizons; controllable action effects; valid responses to interventions; and, for closed-loop use, latency within the control budget. Stochastic futures also require coverage and calibration, unified models require matched evidence that information transfers between reading and writing, and systems built for training, planning, or evaluation must improve decisions in controlled environments or real tasks. Meeting these requirements would move the field from rendering convincing video to modeling how the world changes. 65 Video Foundation Models World-Modeling Lens
